The remainder of this section aims to show and analyze an algorithm that proves Proposition 5.1.

### 5.1 Dividing into Regions

Similar to [duan2023], we consider

$$ \bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}\equiv\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{1}\cdot n}\otimes\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{2}\cdot n}\otimes\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{3}\cdot n} $$

for $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\geq 0$ and $A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3}=1$ . We call each of the three factors of the above tensor product a region. For $r\in[3]$ , we denote the $r$ -th region as

$$ \mathcal{T}^{(r)}\coloneqq\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{r}\cdot n}. $$

The idea is to apply asymmetric hashing on the three regions separately. We will use asymmetric hashing that shares level- $\ell$ $Z$ -blocks in the first region, $Y$ -blocks in the second region, and $X$ -blocks in the third region. Each region will be degenerated into independent copies of a level- $\ell$ interface tensor and the output will be the tensor product of the independent copies of the three level- $\ell$ interface tensors from the three regions. Thus we can analyze each region independently and we only give the detailed analysis on the first region as the analysis for the other two regions follow by symmetry.

From now on, we will describe the analysis on $\mathcal{T}^{(1)}$ in which the level- $\ell$ $Z$ -variable blocks are shared and we will omit the superscript $(1)$ on all variables for conciseness.

### 5.2 Asymmetric Hashing

Recall that $\alpha$ is a distribution on $\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3}\mid i+j+k=2^{\ell}\}$ , i.e., it can be viewed as a distribution on level- $\ell$ constituent tensors. Recall that $\alpha$ induces marginal distributions ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ . We first zero out $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -blocks that are not consistent with the marginals ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ respectively. Let $N_{\textup{BX}}$ be the number of remaining level- $\ell$ $X$ -blocks, and it is not difficult to see that

$$ N_{\textup{BX}}=2^{H({\alpha}_{\textit{X}})\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}. $$

Similarly, let $N_{\textup{BY}}$ and $N_{\textup{BZ}}$ be the number of remaining $Y$ - and $Z$ -blocks, and we have

$$ N_{\textup{BY}}=2^{H({\alpha}_{\textit{Y}})\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)},\quad N_{\textup{BZ}}=2^{H({\alpha}_{\textit{Z}})\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}. $$

Let $N_{\alpha}$ be the number of remaining block triples that are consistent with $\alpha$ . We have

$$ N_{\alpha}=2^{H(\alpha)\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}. $$

Finally, let $N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}$ be the number of remaining block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ .

#### Claim 5.4.

$N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}=2^{(H(\alpha)+P_{\alpha})\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}$ .

#### Proof.

Recall that $P_{\alpha}=\max_{\alpha^{\prime}\in D}H(\alpha^{\prime})-H(\alpha)$ where $D$ is the set of distributions whose marginal distributions on the three dimensions are ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ respectively.

As we zeroed out $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -blocks based on ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ respectively, all remaining block triples are consistent with one of the distributions $\alpha^{\prime}\in D$ . Additionally, $\alpha^{\prime}(i,j,k)\cdot A_{1}\cdot n$ must be an integer for every $i,j,k$ . Let us denote the set of distributions satisfying such properties as $D^{\prime}$ .

Thus, $N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}=\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}\in D^{\prime}}2^{H(\alpha^{\prime})\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}$ . As $|D^{\prime}|=\poly(n)$ , we have that

$$ N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}=2^{(\max_{\alpha^{\prime}\in D^{\prime}}H(\alpha^{\prime}))\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}. $$

When $n$ approaches $\infty$ , the difference between $\max_{\alpha^{\prime}\in D^{\prime}}H(\alpha^{\prime})$ and $\max_{\alpha^{\prime}\in D}H(\alpha^{\prime})$ will approach $0$ , as the entropy function $H$ is continuous. Thus,

$$ N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}=2^{(\max_{\alpha^{\prime}\in D}H(\alpha^{\prime}))\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}=2^{(H(\alpha)+P_{\alpha})\cdot A_{1}n\pm o(n)}.\qed $$

Let $M\in[M_{0},2M_{0}]$ be a prime number for some integer $M_{0}$ . The value of $M_{0}$ is yet to be fixed, but we first require that

$$ M_{0}\geq 8\cdot\max\left\{\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BX}}},\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BY}}}\right\}. $$

One additional term that lower bounds $M_{0}$ will be mentioned later.

We independently pick uniformly random elements $b_{0},\{w_{t}\}_{t=0}^{n}\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ , and define the following hash functions $h_{X},h_{Y},h_{Z}:\{0,\ldots,2^{\ell}\}^{n}\rightarrow\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ :

$$ \displaystyle h_{X}(I) \displaystyle=b_{0}+\left(\sum_{t=1}^{n}w_{t}\cdot I_{t}\right)\bmod M, \displaystyle h_{Y}(J) \displaystyle=b_{0}+\left(w_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{n}w_{t}\cdot J_{t}\right)\bmod M, \displaystyle h_{Z}(K) \displaystyle=b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\left(w_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{n}w_{t}\cdot(2^{\ell}-K_{t})\right)\bmod M. $$

Let $B$ be a Salem-Spencer subset of $\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ that has size $M^{1-o(1)}$ and does not contain any nontrivial $3$ -term arithmetic progressions (modulo $M$ ). Then we zero out all blocks $X_{I}$ with $h_{X}(I)\notin B$ , $Y_{J}$ with $h_{Y}(J)\notin B$ , and $Z_{K}$ with $h_{Z}(K)\notin B$ .

For every block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ in $\mathcal{T}$ , we have that $X_{t}+Y_{t}+Z_{t}=2^{\ell}$ for every $t\in[n]$ . Therefore, it is not difficult to verify that $h_{X}(I)+h_{Y}(J)\equiv 2h_{Z}(K)\pmod{M}$ . In order for $h_{X}(I),h_{Y}(J),h_{Z}(K)\in B$ , we must have $h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b$ for some $b$ , because $B$ does not contain any nontrivial $3$ -term arithmetic progression (modulo $M$ ). We say that triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ with $h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b$ are contained in bucket $b$ .

For every bucket $b$ , if it contains two level- $\ell$ triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ and $X_{I}Y_{J^{\prime}}Z_{K^{\prime}}$ that share the same $X$ -block, then we zero out $X_{I}$ . Similarly, if a bucket contains two level- $\ell$ triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ and $X_{I^{\prime}}Y_{J}Z_{K^{\prime}}$ that share the same level- $\ell$ $Y$ -block, then we zero out $Y_{J}$ . We repeatedly perform the previous zeroing-outs so that eventually, all remaining triples in the same bucket do not share $X$ - or $Y$ -blocks. As each level- $\ell$ block triple in $\mathcal{T}$ must belong to some bucket, we get that all remaining triples do not share $X$ - or $Y$ -blocks, i.e., each level- $\ell$ block $X_{I}$ or $Y_{J}$ is in a unique level- $\ell$ block triple. For every level- $\ell$ block $X_{I}$ (or $Y_{J}$ ), we check whether the unique triple containing it is consistent with the distribution $\alpha$ ; if not, we zero out $X_{I}$ (or $Y_{J}$ ). We call the tensor after this step $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ .

#### Claim 5.5 (Implicit in [cw90], see also [duan2023]).

For a block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}\in\mathcal{T}$ , and for every $b\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ ,

$$ \myPr\left[\vphantom{\sum}h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b\right]=\frac{1}{M^{2}}. $$

Furthermore, for two different block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K},X_{I}Y_{J^{\prime}}Z_{K^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{T}$ that share the same $X$ -block, and for every $b\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ ,

$$ \myPr\left[\vphantom{\sum}h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J^{\prime})=h_{Z}(K^{\prime})=b\;\middle|\;h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b\right]=\frac{1}{M}. $$

This also holds analogously for different block triples that share the same $Y$ -block or $Z$ -block.

#### Claim 5.6.

For every $b\in B$ and for every level- $\ell$ block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}\in\mathcal{T}$ that is consistent with $\alpha$ , the probability that $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ remains in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ conditioned on $h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b$ is $\geq\frac{3}{4}$ .

#### Proof.

The only way that $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ does not remain in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ conditioned on $h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b$ is when some other block triples that share the same $X$ -block or the same $Y$ -block are hashed to the same bucket $b$ .

Right before the hashing step, the total number of block triples remaining is $N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}$ , and the number of $X$ -blocks is $N_{\textup{BX}}$ . By symmetry, each $X$ -block is in the same number of block triples, which is $\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BX}}}$ . Thus, the total number of block triples that share the same $X$ -block as $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is $\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BX}}}-1$ . For each of them, the probability that they are hashed to the same bucket $b$ with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is $\frac{1}{M}$ by Claim 5.5. Therefore, by union bound, the probability that any of them is hashed to the same bucket with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is at most

$$ \frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{M\cdot N_{\textup{BX}}}\leq\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{M_{0}\cdot N_{\textup{BX}}}\;\overset{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eq:global:M_0_bounds_1}}{\leq}\;\frac{1}{8}. $$

Similarly, the probability that any block triple that shares the same level- $\ell$ $Y$ -block is mapped to the same bucket as $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is at most $\frac{1}{8}$ . By union bound, the probability that $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ will be zeroed out is $\leq\frac{1}{4}$ . ∎

#### Claim 5.7.

The expected number of level- $\ell$ block triples in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ is at least

$$ N_{\alpha}\cdot M_{0}^{-1-o(1)}. $$

#### Proof.

For every level- $\ell$ block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}\in\mathcal{T}$ that is consistent with $\alpha$ , and for every $b\in B$ , the probability that $h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b$ is $\frac{1}{M^{2}}$ by Claim 5.5. Also, by Claim 5.6, $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ will remain in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ with probability $\geq\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{M^{2}}$ .

Summing over all block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ and all $b\in B$ , we get that the expected number of block triples in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ is at least

$$ N_{\alpha}\cdot|B|\cdot\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{M^{2}}=N_{\alpha}\cdot M_{0}^{-1-o(1)}.\qed $$

### 5.3 Compatibility Zero-Out I

Recall that $\left\{\beta_{X,i,j,k},\beta_{Y,i,j,k},\beta_{Z,i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ are level- $\ell$ complete split distributions for the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -blocks.

Let

$$ S^{(I,J,K)}_{i,j,k}\coloneqq\{t\in[n]\mid I_{t}=i,J_{t}=j,K_{t}=k\}, $$

and

$$ S^{(K)}_{*,*,k}\coloneqq\{t\in[n]\mid K_{t}=k\}. $$

If clear from the context, we will drop the superscript $(I,J,K)$ or $(K)$ .

Recall that in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ , every level- $\ell$ block $X_{I}$ is in a unique block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ . For every level-1 block $X_{\hat{I}}\in X_{I}$ , we will zero out $X_{\hat{I}}$ if $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I},S_{i,j,k})\neq\beta_{X,i,j,k}$ for any $i,j,k$ (recall the definition of $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I},S_{i,j,k})$ in Definition 3.5). Similarly, every level- $\ell$ block $Y_{J}$ is in a unique block triple, and we zero out every $Y_{\hat{J}}\in Y_{J}$ where $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{J},S_{i,j,k})\neq\beta_{Y,i,j,k}$ for any $i,j,k$ .

We can not perform the same zeroing out for $Z$ -variables, because in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ each level- $\ell$ $Z$ -block is not in a unique block triple and $S_{i,j,k}$ is not well-defined just given the $Z$ -block. Instead, for every level-1 block $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ , we zero out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ if $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k})\neq\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}$ for any $k$ , where

$$ \macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i+j=2^{\ell}-k}\alpha(i,j,k)}\sum_{i+j=2^{\ell}-k}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot\beta_{Z,i,j,k} $$

is the average complete split distribution for constituent tensors whose third coordinate is $k$ .

We call the tensor after the previous zeroing-outs $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{comp}}$ .

Next, we are ready to define the notion of compatibility. The notion is adapted from [duan2023], which is a crucial ingredient in their analysis (and ours).

#### Definition 5.8 (Compatibility).

For some $I,J,K$ , a level-1 block $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ is compatible with a level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ if

- 1. For every $(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3}$ with $i+j+k=2^{\ell},i=0\text{ or }j=0$ , $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ .

- 2. For every index $k\in\{0,1,\ldots,2^{\ell}\}$ , $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k})=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}$ .

#### Claim 5.9.

In $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{comp}}$ , for every level-1 block triple $X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}$ and the level- $\ell$ block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ that contains it, $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ .

#### Proof.

First of all, Item 2 is clearly satisfied, because we zeroed out every $\hat{K}$ with $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k})\neq\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}$ for any $k$ . Next, we show that Item 1 is also satisfied.

Recall that we zeroed out all $X_{\hat{I}}$ where $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I},S_{i,j,k})\neq\beta_{X,i,j,k}$ for any $i,j,k$ . Let $(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}_{\geq 0}$ where $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ and $j=0$ . As $X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}$ remains in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{comp}}$ , $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{X,i,j,k}$ . Because $j=0$ , $J_{t}=0$ for every $t\in S_{i,j,k}$ , which implies that $\bigl(\hat{J}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+1},\,\hat{J}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+2},\,\ldots\,,\,\hat{J}_{t\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)=\vec{0}$ . As $\hat{I}_{\hat{t}}+\hat{J}_{\hat{t}}+\hat{K}_{\hat{t}}=2$ for every $\hat{t}$ , we have that

$$ \bigl(\hat{K}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+1},\,\hat{K}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+2},\,\ldots\,,\,\hat{K}_{t\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)=\vec{2}-\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+1},\,\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+2},\,\ldots\,,\,\hat{I}_{t\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr) $$

for every $t\in S_{i,j,k}$ . Thus, for every $L\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ , the proportion of $L$ appearing in $\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+1},$ $\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+2},\,\ldots\,,\,\hat{I}_{t\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)$ over $t\in S_{i,j,k}$ is exactly the proportion of $\vec{2}-L$ appearing in $\bigl(\hat{K}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+1},$ $\hat{K}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+2},\,\ldots\,,\,\hat{K}_{t\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)$ . In other words, $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})(L)=\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I},S_{i,j,k})(\vec{2}-L)=\beta_{X,i,j,k}(\vec{2}-L)$ . By Remark 5.2, this implies that $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ .

We can show that $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ with $i=0$ similarly. ∎

### 5.4 Compatibility Zero-Out II: Unique Triple

In this step, we zero out level-1 $Z$ -blocks that are compatible with more than one level- $\ell$ triples. To do so, we check if each level-1 $Z$ -block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with multiple level- $\ell$ triples. If so, we zero it out and it becomes a “hole”. Note that after this step, each remaining level-1 $Z$ -block $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ is compatible with a unique level- $\ell$ triple $(X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K})$ containing it.

### 5.5 Usefulness Zero-Out

Next, we further zero out some level-1 $Z$ -blocks using the following definition of usefulness.

#### Definition 5.10 (Usefulness).

For a level-1 block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ and a level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ containing it, if for all $(i,j,k)$ we have $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ , then we say that $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is useful for $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ .

For each $Z_{\hat{K}}$ , it appears in a unique triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ by the previous zeroing out. Furthermore, if $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is not useful for this triple, we zero out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ . We call the current tensor $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}$ .

If there is no hole, then the subtensor of the remaining tensor over $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is isomorphic to

$$ \mathcal{T}^{*}=\bigotimes_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes A_{1}\cdot\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}[\beta_{X,i,j,k},\beta_{Y,i,j,k},\beta_{Z,i,j,k}], $$

i.e., it is the level- $\ell$ interface tensor with parameter list

$$ \left\{\left(A_{1}\cdot\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n,i,j,k,\beta_{X,i,j,k},\beta_{Y,i,j,k},\beta_{Z,i,j,k}\right)\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}. $$

More formally:

#### Claim 5.11.

For any level- $\ell$ block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ contained in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{comp}}$ (or equivalently, $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ ), the subtensor of $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}$ restricted to blocks $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ is a subtensor of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ , where the missing variables in this subtensor are exactly those in level-1 blocks $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that are compatible with multiple level- $\ell$ triples in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{comp}}$ .

#### Proof.

Initially,

$$ \left.\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}\right|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}\equiv\bigotimes_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes A_{1}\cdot\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot n}. $$

To show $\left.\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}\right|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}$ is a subtensor of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ , it suffices to show that the level-1 $X$ -blocks ( $Y$ -blocks or $Z$ -blocks resp.) remaining in $\left.\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}\right|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}$ have the property that $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{X,i,j,k}$ ( $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{J},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Y,i,j,k}$ or $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ resp.) for every $i,j,k$ . This is true because we enforced these constraints on $X$ - and $Y$ -blocks in the compatibility zeroing-out step, and enforced the constraints on $Z$ -blocks by zeroing out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that is not useful for the unique level- $\ell$ triple that contains it. Furthermore, these are the only constraints we have on the level-1 $X$ - and $Y$ -blocks, so the set of $X$ - and $Y$ -variables in $\left.\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}\right|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}$ is the same as that in $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ . It remains to analyze which level-1 $Z$ -blocks are missing in $\left.\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}\right|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}$ .

There are three constraints we enforced on level-1 $Z$ -blocks:

- 1. In the compatibility zeroing-out, we enforced that for every index $k\in\{0,1,\ldots,2^{\ell}\}$ , $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k})=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}$ .

- 2. In the unique triple zeroing-out, we zeroed out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that is compatible with multiple level- $\ell$ triples.

- 3. In the unique triple zeroing-out, we zeroed out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that is not useful for the unique level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ that contains it. Thus, we will have that $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ for every $i,j,k$ if $Z_{\hat{K}}$ remains.

The third constraint implies the first constraint, because if the third constraint holds, then for every $k$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sum_{i,j}\alpha(i,j,k)}\sum_{i+j=2^{\ell}-k}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sum_{i,j}\alpha(i,j,k)}\sum_{i+j=2^{\ell}-k}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot\beta_{Z,i,j,k}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}. $$

Therefore, we can ignore the first condition. As a result, the set of level-1 $Z$ -blocks not in $\left.\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}\right|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}$ but in $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ are exactly those that are compatible with multiple block triples in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{comp}}$ . ∎

Also, note that for different remaining block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ , $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}}$ are level-1-independent, i.e., they do not share the same level-1 blocks. This is because $X_{I}$ and $Y_{J}$ are already in unique level- $\ell$ triples in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ ; for every level-1 block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ , Claim 5.9 shows that $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with every level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ containing it, and then we zeroed out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that are compatible with multiple triples. Thus, every remaining $Z_{\hat{K}}$ in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}$ is contained a unique level- $\ell$ triple as well. As a result, we can write

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}=\bigoplus_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}\;\textup{remaining}}\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}|_{X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}} $$

as a direct sum of broken copies of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ .

### 5.6 Fixing Holes

Next, we analyze the fraction of holes in the broken copies of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ contained in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}$ . To do so, we define the following notion of typicalness, which will then be used to define the quantity $p_{\textup{comp}}$ :

#### Definition 5.12 (Typicalness).

A level-1 $Z$ -block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ in some level- $\ell$ $Z$ -block $Z_{K}$ is typical if $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k})=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}$ for every $k$ . When $Z_{K}$ is consistent with ${\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ , this condition can be equivalently written as $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},[A_{1}n])=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,*}$ , where we recall that $\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,*}=\sum_{i,j,k}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot\beta_{Z,i,j,k}.$

#### Definition 5.13 ( $p_{\textup{comp}}$ ).

For fixed $Z_{\hat{K}}$ and $Z_{K}$ where $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is typical, $p_{\textup{comp}}$ is the probability that a uniformly random block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ consistent with $\alpha$ is compatible with $\hat{K}$ .

By symmetry, this probability is the same for different $Z_{\hat{K}}$ and $Z_{K}$ where $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is typical, so $p_{\textup{comp}}$ is well-defined. Since holes only arise when some $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with multiple triples, the value of $p_{\textup{comp}}$ is closely related to the fraction of holes, and is given by the following claim.

#### Claim 5.14.

The value of $p_{\textup{comp}}$ is

$$ 2^{\left(\lambda_{Z}-H(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,*})+H({\alpha}_{\textit{Z}})\right)A_{1}\cdot n\pm o(n)}, $$

where we recall that

$$ \lambda_{Z}=\sum_{i,j,k:i=0\textup{ or }j=0}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot H(\beta_{Z,i,j,k})+\sum_{k}\alpha(\textup{+},\textup{+},k)\cdot H(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,\textup{+},\textup{+},k}), $$

$$ \alpha(\textup{+},\textup{+},k)=\sum_{i,j>0}\alpha(i,j,k),\quad\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,\textup{+},\textup{+},k}=\frac{1}{\alpha(\textup{+},\textup{+},k)}\sum_{i,j>0}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot\beta_{Z,i,j,k}, $$

and

$$ \macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,*}=\sum_{i,j,k}\alpha(i,j,k)\cdot\beta_{Z,i,j,k}. $$

#### Proof.

By symmetry, it suffices to compute the following two quantities, and $p_{\textup{comp}}$ will be the ratio between them: (1) the number of tuples $(I,J,K,\hat{K})$ where $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is consistent with $\alpha$ , $\hat{K}\in K$ , $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is typical, and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ ; (2) the number of $(I,J,K,\hat{K})$ where $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is consistent with $\alpha$ , $\hat{K}\in K$ , and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is typical.

We first compute the second quantity. First, the number of typical $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is $2^{H(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,*})\cdot A_{1}\cdot n\pm o(n)}$ . Each of these $Z_{\hat{K}}$ uniquely determines a level- $\ell$ block $Z_{K}$ . Also, for each $Z_{K}$ , the number of block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ consistent with $\alpha$ is $\frac{N_{\alpha}}{N_{\textup{BZ}}}=2^{(H(\alpha)-H({\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}))\cdot A_{1}\cdot n\pm o(n)}$ . Therefore, the second quantity is

$$ 2^{(H(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,*})+H(\alpha)-H({\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}))\cdot A_{1}\cdot n\pm o(n)}. $$

Next, we compute the first quantity, which is the number of $(I,J,K,\hat{K})$ where $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is consistent with $\alpha$ , $\hat{K}\in K$ , $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is typical, and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ . By Item 2 in Definition 5.8, if $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with any level- $\ell$ block triple, then it is typical. Thus, we can drop the condition that $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is typical, and equivalently count the number of $(I,J,K,\hat{K})$ where $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ is consistent with $\alpha$ , $\hat{K}\in K$ , and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is compatible with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ .

First, the number of block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ consistent with $\alpha$ is $N_{\alpha}$ . Then, for each such block triple, we count the number of $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ that is compatible with it. If we fix some $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ , then we also have fixed the values of $S_{i,j,k}$ for all $i,j,k$ . Then we can rewrite the condition for $Z_{\hat{K}}$ being compatible with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ equivalently as follows:

#### Definition 5.15 (Compatibility’).

For level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ consistent with $\alpha$ , a level-1 block $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ is compatible with $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ if

- • For every $\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3}\mid i+j+k=2^{\ell},\,i=0\text{ or }j=0\}$ , $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{i,j,k})=\beta_{Z,i,j,k}$ . (This is exactly Item 1 in Definition 5.8).

- • For every $k$ , let $S_{\textup{+},\textup{+},k}\coloneqq\bigcup_{i>0,j>0}S_{i,j,k}$ . Then $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{\textup{+},\textup{+},k})=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,\textup{+},\textup{+},k}$ .

Item 1 and the second condition above imply the original condition $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{*,*,k})=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,*,*,k}$ in Item 2, because

Similar to Theorem 5.3, for every set of complete split distributions $\{\xi_{\textit{W},t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\}_{W,t,r,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ that is at most $\varepsilon$ away in $L_{\infty}$ distance from $\{\beta_{\textit{W},t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\}_{W,t,r,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ , we take an independent copy of the input interface tensor, and degenerate it to independent copies of the output interface tensor with the specified complete split distributions. Let

$$ \xi_{W,t}^{(r)}=\sum_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\alpha_{t}^{(r)}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})\cdot\left(\xi_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\times\xi_{W,t,i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\right)\quad(\forall\,W\in\{X,Y,Z\},\,r\in[3],\,t\in[s^{\prime}]) $$

and $\xi_{W,t}=A_{t,1}\xi_{W,t}^{(1)}+A_{t,2}\xi_{W,t}^{(2)}+A_{t,3}\xi_{W,t}^{(3)}$ be determined by the considered complete split distributions $\{\xi_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\}$ . According to Proposition 6.2, an $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor $\mathcal{T}$ with parameter list $\{(n_{t},i_{t},j_{t},k_{t},\xi_{\textit{X},t},\xi_{\textit{Y},t},\xi_{\textit{Z},t})\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ can degenerate to $2^{E_{1}+E_{2}+E_{3}-o(n)-o_{1/\varepsilon}(n)}$ copies of the target interface tensor. Summing up a copy of the outcome tensor for each $\{\xi_{\textit{W},t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\}_{W,t,r,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ will give the output $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor, so we can get $2^{E_{1}+E_{2}+E_{3}-o(n)-o_{1/\varepsilon}(n)}$ independent copies of the output tensor in total.

It remains to show that $\mathcal{T}$ is a subtensor of the input interface tensor, i.e., a $3\varepsilon$ -interface tensor with parameters $\{(n_{t},i_{t},j_{t},k_{t},\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t})\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ . On the right-hand side of (6), the two complete split distributions have at most $\varepsilon$ distance from $\beta_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ and $\beta_{W,t,i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ , so their product has $\leq 2\varepsilon$ distance44 4 The distance is at most $2\varepsilon$ for the following reason: first, we change $\beta_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ to $\xi_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ , which introduces an additive $\varepsilon$ error (as the right hand side in Section 6 is a weighted average of the entries of $\xi_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ ); then we change $\beta_{W,t,i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ to $\xi_{W,t,i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ , which introduces another additive $\varepsilon$ error. from $\beta_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\times\beta_{W,t,i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}}^{(r)}$ ; since the coefficients $\alpha_{t}^{(r)}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ sum up to 1, we know that the left-hand side $\xi_{\textit{W},t}^{(r)}$ has at most $2\varepsilon$ distance from $\beta_{\textit{W},t}^{(r)}$ as well, and the same holds between $\xi_{\textit{W},t}$ and $\beta_{\textit{W},t}$ . Thus the $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor with complete split distributions $\{\xi_{\textit{W},t}\}_{W,t}$ is contained in the $3\varepsilon$ -interface tensor with $\{\beta_{\textit{W},t}\}_{W,t}$ as a subtensor. Then we conclude the proof. ∎

The remainder of this section aims to prove Proposition 6.2.

### 6.1 Dividing into Regions

For each of the $s^{\prime}$ terms, say the $t$ -th term, we pick three real numbers $A_{t,1},A_{t,2},A_{t,3}\geq 0$ where $A_{t,1}+A_{t,2}+A_{t,3}=1$ , that aims to divide the $t$ -th term in the input level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor into three regions of sizes $A_{t,1}n_{t},A_{t,2}n_{t}$ and $A_{t,3}n_{t}$ respectively. We also pick three different complete split distributions $\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(1)},\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(2)},\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(3)}$ , with the constraint

$$ \beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(1)}A_{t,1}+\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(2)}A_{t,2}+\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(3)}A_{t,3}=\beta_{\textit{X},t}. $$

We also pick $\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(r)}$ and $\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(r)}$ for $r\in[3]$ with similar constraints. Similar to Remark 5.2, we assume without loss of generality that, for every $t,r$ and every $L\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ ,

$$ \beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)}(L)=\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(r)}(\vec{2}-L)\text{ if }j_{t}=0,\quad\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(r)}(L)=\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(r)}(\vec{2}-L)\text{ if }i_{t}=0,\quad\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(r)}(L)=\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)}(\vec{2}-L)\text{ if }k_{t}=0 $$

where $\vec{2}$ denotes the length- $(2^{\ell-1})$ vector whose coordinates are all $2$ , and

$$ \beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)}(L)=0\text{ if }\sum_{t}L_{t}\neq i_{t},\quad\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(r)}(L)=0\text{ if }\sum_{t}L_{t}\neq j_{t},\quad\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(r)}(L)=0\text{ if }\sum_{t}L_{t}\neq k_{t}. $$

For any level- $1$ $X$ -block, if the portion of it in the $r$ -th region of the $t$ -th term is not $\varepsilon$ -approximate consistent with $\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)}$ , we zero it out. We similarly handle level-1 $Y$ -blocks and $Z$ -blocks. It is not hard to see the following.

#### Claim 6.4.

After the previous zeroing-out, we obtain a tensor that is isomorphic to

$$ \bigotimes_{r=1}^{3}\bigotimes_{t=1}^{s^{\prime}}T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes A_{t,r}n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)},\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(r)},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(r)},\varepsilon]. $$

#### Proof.

We only need to show that for a fixed $t$ ,

$$ T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t},\varepsilon]\;\unrhd\;\bigotimes_{r=1}^{3}T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes A_{t,r}n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)},\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(r)},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(r)},\varepsilon] $$

by performing the above zeroing-out rule, i.e., zeroing out every level-1 $X$ -block whose portion in the $r$ -th region is not $\varepsilon$ -approximate consistent with $\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(r)}$ , and doing similarly for $Y$ - and $Z$ -blocks. Suppose some level-1 $X$ -block belongs to the right-hand side and has complete split distributions $\xi_{\textit{X},t}^{(1)},\xi_{\textit{X},t}^{(2)},\xi_{\textit{X},t}^{(3)}$ in three regions respectively, each of which is at most $\varepsilon$ away from $\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(1)},\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(2)},\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(3)}$ in $L_{\infty}$ distance. Then, its average complete split distribution $\xi_{\textit{X},t}\coloneqq A_{1}\xi_{\textit{X},t}^{(1)}+A_{2}\xi_{\textit{X},t}^{(2)}+A_{3}\xi_{\textit{X},t}^{(3)}$ has at most $\varepsilon$ distance from $\beta_{\textit{X},t}$ , which means that the considered level-1 $X$ -block also belong to the left-hand side. It is the same for $Y$ - and $Z$ -blocks, so the right-hand side of (6.1) is a subtensor of the left-hand side, i.e., Eq. (6.1) holds, which further implies the claim. ∎

In the following, we will focus on the first region $r=1$ , in which we will apply asymmetric hashing that allows the sharing of $Z$ -blocks. Let

$$ \mathcal{T}^{(1)}\coloneqq\bigotimes_{t=1}^{s^{\prime}}T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes A_{t,1}n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t}^{(1)},\beta_{\textit{Y},t}^{(1)},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}^{(1)},\varepsilon]. $$

We will omit the superscript $(1)$ on all variables for conciseness.

### 6.2 Asymmetric Hashing

Next, we apply hashing similarly to the global stage. For every $t\in[s^{\prime}]$ , recall that $\alpha_{t}$ is a distribution on $\{(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3}:i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}+k^{\prime}=2^{\ell-1}\}$ . Additionally, the marginal distributions of $\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ on the three dimensions are the same as $\gamma_{\textit{X},t}(i^{\prime},i_{t}-i^{\prime})$ , $\gamma_{\textit{Y},t}(j^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime})$ , $\gamma_{\textit{Z},t}(k^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime})$ , respectively.

Each level- $(\ell-1)$ index sequence is partitioned into $s^{\prime}$ parts, where each part corresponds to one term in $\mathcal{T}$ . The $t$ -th part is a length- $(2n_{t})$ $\{0,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}\}$ -sequence, which can also be viewed as a length- $(n_{t})$ $\{0,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}\}^{2}$ -sequence by combining pairs of adjacent numbers. If the $t$ -th part of a level- $(\ell-1)$ $X$ -index sequence is not consistent with the distribution $\gamma_{\textit{X},t}$ for any $t$ , we zero out the corresponding level- $(\ell-1)$ $X$ -block. We similarly handle the $Y$ - and $Z$ -blocks.

Let $N_{\textup{BX}}$ be the number of remaining level- $(\ell-1)$ $X$ -blocks, and it is not difficult to see that

$$ N_{\textup{BX}}=2^{\sum_{t}H(\gamma_{\textit{X},t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}. $$

Similarly, let $N_{\textup{BY}}$ and $N_{\textup{BZ}}$ be the number of remaining $Y$ - and $Z$ -blocks, and we have

$$ N_{\textup{BY}}=2^{\sum_{t}H(\gamma_{\textit{Y},t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)},\quad N_{\textup{BZ}}=2^{\sum_{t}H(\gamma_{\textit{Z},t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}. $$

Let $N_{\alpha}$ be the number of remaining block triples that are consistent with $\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ . We have

$$ N_{\alpha}=2^{\sum_{t}H(\alpha_{t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}. $$

Finally, let $N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}$ be the number of remaining level- $(\ell-1)$ block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ .

#### Claim 6.5.

$N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}=2^{\sum_{t}(H(\alpha_{t})+P_{\alpha,t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}$ , where we recall that $P_{\alpha,t}\coloneqq\max_{\alpha^{\prime}_{t}\in D_{t}}H(\alpha^{\prime}_{t})-H(\alpha_{t})$ in which $D_{t}$ is the set of distributions sharing the same marginals as $\alpha_{t}$ .

#### Proof.

Fixing a series of distributions $\alpha^{\prime}_{t}\in D_{t}$ ( $t=1,2,\ldots,s^{\prime}$ ), the number of level- $(\ell-1)$ block triples consistent with $\{\alpha^{\prime}_{t}\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ equals

$$ 2^{\sum_{t}H(\alpha^{\prime}_{t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}\;\leq\;2^{\sum_{t}\max_{\alpha^{\prime\prime}_{t}\in D_{t}}H(\alpha^{\prime\prime}_{t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}\;\leq\;2^{\sum_{t}(H(\alpha_{t})+P_{\alpha,t})\cdot A_{t,1}n_{t}\pm o(n)}. $$

Taking summation over all $\poly(n)=2^{o(n)}$ series of distributions $\{\alpha^{\prime}_{t}\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ will prove the claim. ∎

Let $M\in[M_{0},2M_{0}]$ be a prime number for some integer $M_{0}$ . Similar as before, the value of $M_{0}$ is yet to be fixed, but we first require that

$$ M_{0}\geq 8\cdot\max\left\{\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BX}}},\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BY}}}\right\}. $$

We independently pick uniformly random elements $b_{0},\{w_{p}\}_{p=0}^{2n}\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ , and define the following hash functions $h_{X},h_{Y},h_{Z}:\{0,\ldots,2^{\ell-1}\}^{n}\rightarrow\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ :

$$ \displaystyle h_{X}(I) \displaystyle=b_{0}+\left(\sum_{p=1}^{2n}w_{p}\cdot I_{p}\right)\bmod M, \displaystyle h_{Y}(J) \displaystyle=b_{0}+\left(w_{0}+\sum_{p=1}^{2n}w_{p}\cdot J_{p}\right)\bmod M, \displaystyle h_{Z}(K) \displaystyle=b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\left(w_{0}+\sum_{p=1}^{2n}w_{p}\cdot(2^{\ell-1}-K_{p})\right)\bmod M. $$

Next, for a Salem-Spencer subset $B$ of $\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ that has size $M^{1-o(1)}$ , we zero out all level- $(\ell-1)$ blocks $X_{I}$ with $h_{X}(I)\notin B$ , $Y_{J}$ with $h_{Y}(J)\notin B$ , and $Z_{K}$ with $h_{Z}(K)\notin B$ . Then all remaining block triples are contained in a bucket $b$ for some $b\in B$ .

For every bucket $b$ , if it contains two level- $(\ell-1)$ triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ and $X_{I}Y_{J^{\prime}}Z_{K^{\prime}}$ that share the same $X$ -block, then we zero out $X_{I}$ . We similarly handle $Y$ -blocks. We repeatedly perform the previous zeroing-outs so that all remaining triples do not share $X$ - or $Y$ -blocks. For every level- $(\ell-1)$ block $X_{I}$ (or $Y_{J}$ ), we check whether the unique triple containing it is consistent with $\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ ; if not, we zero out $X_{I}$ (or $Y_{J}$ ). We call the tensor after this step $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ .

The following claims, which are analogous to the claims in Section 5, still hold, and we omit their proofs to conciseness.

#### Claim 6.6 (Implicit in [cw90], see also [duan2023]).

For a level- $(\ell-1)$ block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}\in\mathcal{T}$ , and for every $b\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ ,

$$ \myPr\left[\vphantom{\sum}h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b\right]=\frac{1}{M^{2}}. $$

Furthermore, for two different block triples $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K},X_{I}Y_{J^{\prime}}Z_{K^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{T}$ that share the same $X$ -block, and for every $b\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ ,

$$ \myPr\left[\vphantom{\sum}h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J^{\prime})=h_{Z}(K^{\prime})=b\;\middle|\;h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b\right]=\frac{1}{M}. $$

This also holds analogously for different block triples that share the same $Y$ -block or $Z$ -block.

#### Claim 6.7.

For every $b\in B$ and for every level- $(\ell-1)$ block triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}\in\mathcal{T}$ that is consistent with $\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}$ , the probability that $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ remains in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ conditioned on $h_{X}(I)=h_{Y}(J)=h_{Z}(K)=b$ is $\geq\frac{3}{4}$ .

#### Claim 6.8.

The expected number of level- $(\ell-1)$ block triples in $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{hash}}$ is at least $N_{\alpha}\cdot M_{0}^{-1-o(1)}$ .

### 6.3 Compatibility Zero-Out I

Recall that for every $W\in\{X,Y,Z\}$ and $i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}+k^{\prime}=2^{\ell-1}$ , $\beta_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ is a level- $(\ell-1)$ complete split distribution, and they satisfy

$$ \beta_{W,t}=\sum_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})\cdot\left(\beta_{W,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\times\beta_{W,t,i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}}\right). $$

Let

and

$$ S^{(K)}_{t,*,*,k^{\prime}}:=\{p\textup{ is in the $t$-th term}\mid K_{p}=k^{\prime}\},\quad S_{t,*,*,*}:=\{p\textup{ is in the $t$-th term}\}. $$

If clear from the context, we will drop the superscript $(I,J,K)$ or $(K)$ .

For every level- $1$ block $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ , we zero out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ if $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{t,*,*,k^{\prime}})\neq\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{Z,t,*,*,k^{\prime}}$ for any $t,k^{\prime}$ , where

### 6.4 Compatibility Zero-Out II: Unique Triple

In this step, we zero out all level- $1$ $Z$ -block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that are compatible with more than one level- $(\ell-1)$ triples and they become holes. After this step, each remaining level- $1$ $Z$ -block $Z_{\hat{K}}\in Z_{K}$ is compatible with a unique level- $(\ell-1)$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ containing it.

### 6.5 Usefulness Zero-Out

Next, we further zero out some level-1 $Z$ -blocks using the following definition of usefulness.

#### Definition 6.11 (Usefulness).

For a level-1 block $Z_{\hat{K}}$ and a level- $(\ell-1)$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ containing it, if for all $t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}$ we have $\textsf{{split}}(\hat{K},S_{t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}})=\beta_{Z,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}$ , then we say that $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is useful for $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ .

For each $Z_{\hat{K}}$ , it appears in a unique triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ by the previous zeroing out. Furthermore, if $Z_{\hat{K}}$ is not useful for this triple, we zero out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ . We call the current tensor $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}$ .

Ideally, we want the subtensor of $\mathcal{T}_{\textup{useful}}$ over each triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ to be isomorphic to

$$ \mathcal{T}^{*}=\bigotimes_{t\in[s^{\prime}]}\;\bigotimes_{i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}+k^{\prime}=2^{\ell-1}}T_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}^{\otimes A_{t,1}\cdot(\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})+\alpha_{t}(i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}))\cdot n_{t}}[\beta_{X,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}},\beta_{Y,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}},\beta_{Z,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}]. $$

However, there will be two types of holes. The first type of holes is caused by the fact that some level- $1$ subtensors are already missing in the input tensor because we enforced complete split distributions $\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}$ on it; the second type of holes is caused by zeroing out $Z_{\hat{K}}$ that are compatible with multiple level- $(\ell-1)$ triples. In the next section, we will analyze and fix these two types of holes.

### 6.6 Fixing Holes

First, we analyze the fraction of holes that are caused by the complete split distributions enforced in the input. To do so, we focus on a fixed triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ and the subtensor $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ we desire. Then we take a random level- $1$ block that is not zeroed out in $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ , and upper bound the probability that this level- $1$ block is zeroed out in the input level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor. By symmetry, it suffices to focus on $X$ -blocks.

Fix any $(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ , let us analyze the fraction of its occurrences in a random level- $1$ $X$ -block in $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ . For every $t\in[s^{\prime}]$ , and for every $i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}$ , we first focus on the level- $\ell$ positions in the $t$ -th term where $(i_{t},j_{t},k_{t})$ is split into $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ and $(i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime})$ (thus, there are $A_{t,1}\cdot\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})\cdot n_{t}$ such positions). Among these positions, we want to analyze the number of positions that correspond to the level- $1$ chunk $(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ . Therefore, the first half-chunk, which corresponds to $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ , should be $(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}})$ , and the second half-chunk, which corresponds to $(i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime})$ , should be $(\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}+1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ .

There are $A_{t,1}\cdot(\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})+\alpha_{t}(i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}))\cdot n_{t}$ level- $(\ell-1)$ positions corresponding to $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ , and among them, $A_{t,1}\cdot\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})\cdot n_{t}$ are in odd positions. By definition of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ , the fraction of $(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}})$ in these $A_{t,1}\cdot(\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})+\alpha_{t}(i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime}))\cdot n_{t}$ positions is $\beta_{X,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}})$ , and if we take a random level- $1$ $X$ -block in $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ , the fraction of $(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}})$ among the odd positions corresponding to $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ is $\beta_{X,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}(\hat{i}_{1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}})\pm o(1)$ with $1-1/\poly(n)$ probability, by concentration bounds. Furthermore, the subset of positions in these $A_{t,1}\cdot\alpha_{t}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})\cdot n_{t}$ positions is also random. Similarly, with $1-1/\poly(n)$ probability, the fraction of $(\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}+1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ in the even positions corresponding to $(i_{t}-i^{\prime},j_{t}-j^{\prime},k_{t}-k^{\prime})$ is $\beta_{X,t,i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}(\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-2}+1},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\pm o(1)$ , and the positions are also random. ## 7 Fixing Holes

In this section, we show (by generalizing a result by Duan [duanpersonal]) that we can degenerate a direct sum of some broken copies of an interface tensor into an unbroken copy of the same tensor as long as we only have a small fraction of holes in the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -dimensions. Since our result of fixing holes in all $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables might be of independent interest, we present our result in a more general setting.

Let us first describe the setup of this section. We consider a partitioned tensor $T$ on variable sets $X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N_{X}}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{N_{Y}}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{1},\dots,z_{N_{Z}}\}$ of size $|X|=N_{X}$ , $|Y|=N_{Y}$ , $|Z|=N_{Z}$ with partitions $X=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{M_{X}}X_{i}$ , $Y=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{M_{Y}}Y_{k}$ , $Z=\bigsqcup_{k=1}^{M_{Z}}Z_{k}$ into equal-size parts $|X_{i}|=m_{X}$ for all $i\in[M_{X}]$ , $|Y_{j}|=m_{Y}$ for all $j\in[M_{Y}]$ , and $|Z_{k}|=m_{Z}$ for all $k\in[M_{K}]$ . (We use the notation $X_{i}$ to represent both the part itself and the set of elements in this part.) Let $\mathcal{P}_{X}=\{X_{i}\mid i\in[M_{X}]\}$ denote the set of parts in the partition of $X$ , and similarly let $\mathcal{P}_{Y},\mathcal{P}_{Z}$ denote the set of parts in the partition of $Y$ and $Z$ respectively. Note that by definition $N_{X}=M_{X}\cdot m_{X}$ , $N_{Y}=M_{Y}\cdot m_{Y}$ , $N_{Z}=M_{Z}\cdot m_{Z}$ and $|\mathcal{P}_{X}|=M_{X}$ , $|\mathcal{P}_{Y}|=M_{Y}$ , $|\mathcal{P}_{Z}|=M_{Z}$ .

We consider the broken copies of $T$ where some of the $X$ -, $Y$ - and $Z$ -parts are missing which we call the holes. (Equivalently, the variables in a part are either all present or all missing.) More specifically, we say that $T_{\textup{hole}}$ is a broken copy of $T$ with holes $P^{(0)}_{X}\subseteq M_{X}$ , $P^{(0)}_{Y}\subseteq M_{Y}$ , $P^{(0)}_{Z}\subseteq M_{Z}$ when

$$ T_{\textup{hole}}\;=\;T\big|_{X\setminus\bigsqcup_{X_{t}\in P^{(0)}_{X}}X_{t},\;Y\setminus\bigsqcup_{Y_{t}\in P^{(0)}_{Y}}Y_{t},\;Z\setminus\bigsqcup_{Z_{t}\in P^{(0)}_{Z}}Z_{t}} $$

is obtained from $T$ via zeroing out the variables in the parts $P^{(0)}_{X}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{X}$ , $P^{(0)}_{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{Y}$ , $P^{(0)}_{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{Z}$ . For simplicity, we define the notation

$$ T\|_{P_{X},\,P_{Y},\,P_{Z}}\;\coloneqq\;T\big|_{\bigsqcup_{X_{t}\in P_{X}}X_{t},\;\bigsqcup_{Y_{t}\in P_{Y}}Y_{t},\;\bigsqcup_{Z_{t}\in P_{Z}}Z_{t}} $$

to represent the subtensor of $T$ over the set of parts $P_{X},P_{Y},P_{Z}$ . With this notation, Section 7 can be rewritten as

$$ T_{\mathrm{hole}}\;=\;T\big\|_{\mathcal{P}_{X}\setminus P^{(0)}_{X},\;\mathcal{P}_{Y}\setminus P^{(0)}_{Y},\;\mathcal{P}_{Z}\setminus P^{(0)}_{Z}}. $$

We call the ratios $\bigl\lvert P^{(0)}_{X}\bigr\rvert\big/M_{X}$ , $\bigl\lvert P^{(0)}_{Y}\bigr\rvert\big/M_{Y}$ , $\bigl\lvert P^{(0)}_{Z}\bigr\rvert\big/M_{Z}$ the fraction of holes in the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -dimension respectively.

We will show that we can degenerate sub-polynomially many broken copies of $T$ with small fraction of holes in all three dimensions into an unbroken copy of $T$ if $T$ satisfies the following property.

#### Property 7.1.

There exists a subset $\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{N_{X}}\times\mathcal{S}_{N_{Y}}\times\mathcal{S}_{N_{Z}}$ of permutations over the variables of $T$ where $\mathcal{S}_{N}$ denotes the symmetric group on $[N]$ , such that $\mathcal{G}$ satisfies the following:

- 1. Every $(\pi_{X},\pi_{Y},\pi_{Z})\in\mathcal{G}$ preserves the partitions. Specifically, it permutes any part into some entire part, i.e., for every part $X_{t}\in\mathcal{P}_{X}$ , there exists $X_{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{P}_{X}$ such that $\pi_{X}(X_{t})\coloneqq\{\pi_{X}(x)\mid x\in X_{t}\}=X_{t^{\prime}}$ . Similar conditions hold for $Y$ - and $Z$ -parts. Hence, $\pi_{X},\pi_{Y},\pi_{Z}$ also induce permutations on $\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{Y},\mathcal{P}_{Z}$ , respectively.

- 2. Every $(\pi_{X},\pi_{Y},\pi_{Z})\in\mathcal{G}$ preserves the tensor structure of $T$ . Formally, the coefficient of $x_{i}\cdot y_{j}\cdot z_{k}$ in $T$ equals the coefficient of $\pi_{X}(x_{i})\cdot\pi_{Y}(y_{j})\cdot\pi_{Z}(z_{k})$ in $T$ , for all variables $x_{i},y_{j},z_{k}$ .

- 3. A uniformly random element $(\pi_{X},\pi_{Y},\pi_{Z})\in\mathcal{G}$ permutes any given part to a uniform random part. Formally, for any fixed $X_{t},X_{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{P}_{X}$ , $Y_{t},Y_{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{P}_{Y}$ , $Z_{t},Z_{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{P}_{Z}$ , and for a uniformly random $(\pi_{X},\pi_{Y},\pi_{Z})\in\mathcal{G}$ , we have $\displaystyle\myPr[\pi_{X}(X_{t})=X_{t^{\prime}}]$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M_{X}},$ $\displaystyle\myPr[\pi_{Y}(Y_{t})=Y_{t^{\prime}}]$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M_{Y}},$ $\displaystyle\myPr[\pi_{Z}(Z_{t})=Z_{t^{\prime}}]$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M_{Z}}.$

# More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication

## Abstract

We present a new improvement on the laser method for designing fast matrix multiplication algorithms. The new method further develops the recent advances by [Duan, Wu, Zhou FOCS 2023] and [Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu, Zhou SODA 2024]. Surprisingly the new improvement is achieved by incorporating more asymmetry in the analysis, circumventing a fundamental tool of prior work that requires two of the three dimensions to be treated identically. Together with recent advances in numerical optimization [Dupont et al. arXiv:2608.16884], the method yields a new bound on the square matrix multiplication exponent

improved from the previous bound of $\omega<2.371552$ . We also improve the bounds of the exponents for multiplying rectangular matrices of various shapes.

## 1 Introduction

Multiplication of matrices is a fundamental algebraic primitive with applications throughout computer science and beyond. The study of its algorithmic complexity has been a vibrant area in theoretical computer science and mathematics ever since Strassen’s [Str69] 1969 discovery that the rank of 2 by 2 matrix multiplication is $7$ (and not $8$ ), leading to the first truly subcubic, $O(n^{2.81})$ -time algorithm for multiplying $n\times n$ matrices. Fifty-five years later, researchers are still attempting to lower the exponent $\omega$ , defined as the smallest real number for which $n\times n$ matrices can be multiplied in $O(n^{\omega+\varepsilon})$ time for all $\varepsilon>0$ .

After many decades of work (e.g. [Str69, Pan78, BCRL79, Sch81, Rom82, CW82, Str86, CW90, DS13, Vas12, LG14, AV21, DWZ23, VXXZ24]), the current best bound $\omega<2.371552$ was given by [VXXZ24] optimizing a recent approach by Duan, Wu, and Zhou [DWZ23].

There is a straightforward lower bound of $\omega\geq 2$ since the output size is $n^{2}$ . No larger lower bound is known, leading many to optimistically conjecture that $\omega=2$ . Unfortunately, several papers [AFLG15, BCC+17b, BCC+17a, AV18a, Alm21, AV18b, CVZ21] prove significant limitations to all known approaches for designing matrix multiplication algorithms. The most general limitations [Alm21, AV18b, CVZ21] say that even major generalizations of the known approaches cannot prove $\omega=2$ . The most restricted limitation [AFLG15] focuses on the laser method defined by Strassen [Str86] and applied to the powers of a very particular tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{5}$ defined by Coppersmith and Winograd [CW90]. This is the method that all the best results11 1 Coppersmith and Winograd’s paper [CW90] technically used $\mathrm{CW}_{6}$ instead of $\mathrm{CW}_{5}$ , but the limitation of [AFLG15] on $\mathrm{CW}_{6}$ is actually worse than those for $\mathrm{CW}_{5}$ . from the last 38 years have used. The limitation says that the laser method on $\mathrm{CW}_{5}$ cannot prove that $\omega<2.3078$ . All papers on matrix multiplication algorithms from the last 10 years or so have been focused on bringing the $\omega$ upper bound closer to this $2.3078$ lower bound.

The main contribution of this paper is a new improvement over the laser method when applied to the powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{5}$ . The new method builds upon work of [DWZ23] and [VXXZ24] and yields new improved bounds on $\omega$ and several rectangular matrix multiplication exponents22 2 The constraint programs that our new method leads to are significantly larger and more complex than in prior work. The nonlinear solver we are using struggles, and it can take many days for it to get a solution for any fixed $\omega(1,k,1)$ . Unfortunately, we were not able to solve the constraint program for the value $\alpha$ studied by Coppersmith [Cop82, Cop97] defined as the largest number such that $n$ by $n^{\alpha}$ by $n$ matrix multiplication can be done in $O(n^{2+\varepsilon})$ time for all $\varepsilon>0$ . $\omega(1,k,1)$ defined as the smallest real value for which $n\times n^{k}$ by $n^{k}\times n$ matrix multiplication can be done in $O(n^{\omega(1,k,1)+\varepsilon})$ time for all $\varepsilon>0$ ; the previous best bounds for rectangular matrix multiplication were by [LG24, VXXZ24].

Our results are summarized in Table 1. Our new bound on $\omega$ is

$$ \omega<2.371339, $$

improved from the previous bound by [VXXZ24] of $\omega<2.371552$ , inching towards the lower bound of $2.3078$ . A recent work [DEK+26] further improves the bound derived from our method to

$$ \omega<2.371177. $$

As in prior works, our method reduces the search for the best bound on $\omega$ to a nonlinear optimization problem (see Section 7); [DEK+26] solve this optimization problem at a larger scale using modern optimization and machine learning techniques, leading to the new bound based on the same algorithm and analysis as in this paper.

As a specific example for a rectangular matrix multiplication exponent, we obtain a new bound for the exponent $\mu$ satisfying the equation $\omega(1,\mu,1)=1+2\mu$ . The previous bound from [VXXZ24] was $\mu<0.527661$ and we improve it to $\mu<0.5275$ . The value $\mu$ is a key part of the best known running times of several important problems, including All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) in unweighted directed graphs [Zwi02], computing minimum witnesses of Boolean Matrix Multiplication [CKL07], and All-Pairs Bottleneck Paths in node-weighted graphs [SYZ11]. Our new bound implies that all the aforementioned problems can be solved in $O(n^{2.5275})$ time, improving on the previous known running time of $O(n^{2.527661})$ .
