## 2 Technical Overview

In this section, we give a high-level overview of recent algorithms for matrix multiplication and the new ideas we introduce in this paper for further improvement. We assume familiarity with notions related to tensors and matrix multiplication; the unfamiliar reader may want to read the preliminaries in Section 3 below first. Afterward, in Section 4, we give a more detailed overview of how we design our new algorithm.

### 2.1 The Laser Method and Asymptotic Sum Inequality

In order to design a matrix multiplication algorithm, using Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality [Sch81], it suffices to give an upper bound on the asymptotic rank of a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors. However, directly bounding the rank of a matrix multiplication tensor is quite difficult (for example, even determining the rank of the tensor for multiplying $3\times 3$ matrices is still an open problem today), and so algorithms since the work of Coppersmith and Winograd [CW90] have used an indirect approach:

- 1. Start with the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , which is known to have minimal asymptotic rank.

- 2. Take a large Kronecker power $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes n}$ , which must therefore also have a small (asymptotic) rank.

- 3. Use the laser method to show that $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes n}$ has a zeroing out33 3 If $T$ is a tensor over $X,Y,Z$ , a zeroing out of $T$ is a tensor obtained by picking subsets $X^{\prime}\subseteq X$ , $Y^{\prime}\subseteq Y$ , $Z^{\prime}\subseteq Z$ , and restricting $T$ to only those subsets. to a large direct sum $S$ of matrix multiplication tensors.

- 4. Since zeroing out cannot increase the tensor rank, this shows that $S$ has a small (asymptotic) rank, and then we can apply Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality.

The laser method in Step 3 is a tool introduced by Strassen [Str87] for converting Kronecker powers of tensors into direct sums of matrix multiplication tensors. All improvements since Coppersmith and Winograd’s algorithm have used this approach [DS13, Vas12, LG14, AV21, DWZ23, VXXZ24], focusing on improving the use of the laser method to yield a larger direct sum $S$ of larger matrix multiplication tensors, and this is the step which we improve here as well. The laser method is a general tool which applies to any tensor $T$ that has been partitioned in a particular way. Let us first introduce some relevant notations.

Suppose $T$ is a tensor over $X,Y,Z$ , and we partition $X=\bigsqcup_{i}X_{i}$ , $Y=\bigsqcup_{j}Y_{j}$ , and $Z=\bigsqcup_{k}Z_{k}$ and define the subtensor $T_{i,j,k}$ as $T$ restricted to $X_{i},Y_{j},Z_{k}$ . Thus, $T$ is partitioned as $T=\sum_{i,j,k}T_{i,j,k}$ . The laser method requires this partition to have additional structure44 4 Namely, there must be an integer $p$ such that $T_{i,j,k}=0$ whenever $i+j+k\neq p$ . In the case of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , we will use a partition with $p=2$ . which we will not focus on in this overview. Notably, when we take a Kronecker power $T^{\otimes n}$ , which is a tensor over $X^{n},Y^{n},Z^{n}$ , this can also be partitioned as $T^{\otimes n}=\sum_{I,J,K}T_{IJK}$ where $I,J,K$ are vectors of length $n$ , and $T_{IJK}\coloneqq\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^{n}T_{I_{\ell},J_{\ell},K_{\ell}}$ is a tensor over $X_{I}:=\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}X_{I_{\ell}}$ , $Y_{J}:=\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}Y_{J_{\ell}}$ , and $Z_{K}:=\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}Z_{K_{\ell}}$ .

Consider a probability distribution $\alpha$ on the subtensors of $T$ , which assigns probability $\alpha_{ijk}$ to subtensor $T_{i,j,k}$ . In the Kronecker power $T^{\otimes n}$ , we can zero out according to the marginals of $\alpha$ . For instance, we zero out $X_{I}\subset X^{n}$ unless, for all $i$ , we have $\frac{1}{n}\cdot|\{\ell\in[n]\mid I_{\ell}=i\}|=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{ijk}$ . Assuming $\alpha$ is uniquely determined by its marginals (which is often not the case, as we will discuss more later), this means $T^{\otimes n}$ has been zeroed out so that every remaining $T_{IJK}$ is a copy (up to permutation of indices) of the tensor $B=\bigotimes_{i,j,k}T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes\alpha_{ijk}\cdot n}$ .

Summarizing, we have so far zeroed out $T^{\otimes n}$ into a sum of many copies of the tensor $B$ (one copy of $B$ from each $T_{IJK}$ ). However, this is not a direct sum. Indeed, for example, there can be many remaining $T_{IJK}$ and $T_{I^{\prime}J^{\prime}K^{\prime}}$ with $I=I^{\prime}$ , which both use $X_{I}$ .

The main result of the laser method is that a further, carefully-chosen zeroing out can result in a direct sum of copies of the tensor $B$ , where each two remaining $T_{IJK}$ and $T_{I^{\prime}J^{\prime}K^{\prime}}$ have $I\neq I^{\prime}$ , $J\neq J^{\prime}$ , and $K\neq K^{\prime}$ . Moreover, this further zeroing out only removes a small number of $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ , so that a large number of copies of $B$ remain. (The exact number is a combinatorial expression in terms of the marginals of $\alpha$ which we will discuss in more detail in later sections.)

When this method is applied to $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , each subtensor is in fact a matrix multiplication tensor, so $B$ is also a matrix multiplication tensor. Thus, the output of the laser method can be directly given to the asymptotic sum inequality.

### 2.2 Recursive Applications of the Laser Method to Tensor Powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$

Coppersmith and Winograd [CW90] then noticed that the laser method can yield improved results when applied to the Kronecker square, $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2}$ .

Roughly speaking, the intuition is that the square gives us more freedom to pick the partition that is needed to apply the laser method, since Kronecker squares of the partitions of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ correspond to only a subset of the possible partitions of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2}$ . Coppersmith and Winograd take advantage of this, and pick a partition of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2}$ which allows the tensors $T_{IJK}$ to become larger. In fact, compared to the partition obtained from analyzing $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2n}$ , the partition from analyzing $(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes n}$ is a coarsening of the previous partition (where, for instance, each $X_{I}$ now is a union of possibly multiple previous $X_{I}$ ’s). Thus, $T_{IJK}$ , which is a tensor over the variable blocks $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ , is now larger. If the tensors $T_{IJK}$ ’s were all matrix multiplication tensors, then the asymptotic sum inequality tends to give better bounds when they are larger. However, in this new partition, each subtensor is no longer a matrix multiplication tensor. In other words, the laser method still yields a direct sum of copies of $B=\bigotimes_{i,j,k}T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes\alpha_{ijk}\cdot n}$ , but $B$ is not a matrix multiplication tensor, so the asymptotic sum inequality cannot be directly applied.

Coppersmith and Winograd solved this by applying the laser method recursively. They first applied the laser method to each subtensor $T_{i,j,k}$ which is not a matrix multiplication tensor, showing that $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes m}$ for large $m$ can zero out into direct sums of matrix multiplication tensors. Then, since the tensor $B$ is a Kronecker product of such powers, this can be used to zero out into a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors.

The next few improvements to $\omega$ [DS13, Vas12, LG14] applied this recursive laser method approach to $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ for larger and larger integers $\ell\geq 1$ . Similar to before, there is a natural partition $X=\bigsqcup_{i}X_{i}$ , $Y=\bigsqcup_{j}Y_{j}$ , and $Z=\bigsqcup_{k}Z_{k}$ of the variables from the base tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ , and products of $X_{i}$ ’s, $Y_{j}$ ’s or $Z_{k}$ ’s form subsets of variables $X_{I}$ ’s, $Y_{J}$ ’s, or $Z_{K}$ ’s in $(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}})^{\otimes n}$ . We will call each subset of variables $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ a level- $\ell$ variable block and we call a subtensor obtained from restricting to some level- $\ell$ variable blocks a level- $\ell$ subtensor. Since the level- $\ell$ partition is a coarsening of the level- $(\ell-1)$ partition, each level- $\ell$ variable block is the union of possibly many level- $(\ell-1)$ variable blocks induced by the natural partition of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-2}}$ , and consequently each level- $\ell$ subtensor is the sum of many level- $(\ell-1)$ subtensors. As $\ell$ increases, the task of applying the laser method to increasingly more intricate subtensors becomes more difficult, and significant algorithmic and computational challenges arise.

The next improvement [AV21] focused on the case when the marginals of $\alpha$ do not uniquely determine $\alpha$ . In this case, there is a corresponding penalty that reduces the number of copies of $B$ the laser method can achieve, and [AV21] showed a new approach to reduce this penalty.

### 2.3 Asymmetry and Combination Loss

All improvements to the laser method thus far would apply equally well to any tensor with an appropriate partition. The next, recently improved algorithm [DWZ23] focused on improving the recursive use of the laser method specifically when it is applied to the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ in the recursive fashion described above.

The key observation, referred to as “combination loss” in their paper, is as follows. Above, in order to ensure that the laser method gave a direct sum of copies of $B$ , previous works ensured that any two remaining level- $\ell$ subtensors do not share any level- $\ell$ variable blocks $X_{I}$ , $Y_{J}$ or $Z_{K}$ . For $\ell=1$ , namely when the laser method is applied to the first power of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , this is both necessary and sufficient, because the level- $1$ subtensors are matrix multiplication tensors which use the entire level-1 variable blocks, so any two sharing an $I$ , $J$ , or $K$ must intersect.

However, for $\ell>1$ , the laser method needs to be applied recursively to every level- $k$ subtensor for $k=\ell,\,\ell\!-\!1,\dots,1$ . This means that by the end of the algorithm, we are potentially only using a small fraction of the variables in the level- $\ell$ subtensor rather than the entire subtensor. So it is possible that even if two level- $\ell$ subtensors $T_{IJK}$ and $T_{I^{\prime}J^{\prime}K}$ share the same level- $\ell$ $Z$ -variable block $Z_{K}$ in the beginning, after recursive applications of the laser method, the subtensors of $T_{IJK}$ and $T_{I^{\prime}J^{\prime}K}$ which remain after zeroing out into matrix multiplication tensors may use disjoint subsets of $Z_{K}$ , i.e., they may be independent. In this case, we could keep both $T_{IJK}$ and $T_{I^{\prime}J^{\prime}K}$ when we apply the laser method to $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ and still have a direct sum of subtensors, contrary to what was done in the previous algorithms where only one could be kept.

In order to benefit from this observation, one major issue is that when $T_{IJK}$ and $T_{I^{\prime}J^{\prime}K}$ are each zeroed out to their desired subtensors via the recursive applications of the laser method, they may each zero out parts of $Z_{K}$ that are meant to be used by the other. Thus it is unclear how to control and analyze the recursive procedure so that we maximize the number of these subtensors remaining in the end while ensuring that they are indeed independent.

However, for the $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ tensor, Duan, Wu, and Zhou in [DWZ23] observed that the issue can be partially overcome. In particular, they were able to allow two level- $\ell$ subtensors to share level- $\ell$ variable blocks in the $Z$ -dimension as long as they had the guarantee that any two level- $\ell$ subtensors do not share any level- $\ell$ blocks in the $X$ - or $Y$ -dimension. Due to the special structure of the $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ tensor, it turns out that by ensuring independence among level- $\ell$ $X$ - and $Y$ -blocks, we can obtain sufficient information about the level- $(\ell-1)$ structure of $Z$ -blocks in level- $\ell$ subtensors. Therefore, by introducing asymmetry via treating the $Z$ -variables differently from the $X$ - and $Y$ -variables, [DWZ23] obtained a procedure that obtains a collection of level- $\ell$ subtensors that do not share any level- $(\ell-1)$ $Z$ -variable blocks, so they are independent. The follow-up work [VXXZ24] further generalized the techniques presented in [DWZ23] and allowed the sharing of level- $(\ell-1)$ $Z$ -variable blocks. In fact, their approach only requires that each level- $1$ $Z$ -variable block belongs to a unique remaining level- $\ell$ subtensor $T_{IJK}$ . This allowed them to obtain an improvement since each subtensor $T_{IJK}$ can use a more “fine-grained” subset of $Z$ -variables.

A priori, it is perhaps surprising that such an asymmetric approach, applied to the very symmetric Coppersmith-Winograd tensor, leads to an improved algorithm. In previous work, much effort was devoted to ensuring that the algorithm was entirely symmetric with respect to the $X,Y,Z$ -dimensions. For instance, many intermediate steps of the laser method require taking the minimum of three quantities depending separately on $X,Y,Z$ (like the entropies of the three marginal distributions of $\alpha$ ), and picking a symmetric distribution prevents losses in these steps. Similarly, in the design of algorithms for rectangular matrix multiplication using the laser method [LG12, LGU18, VXXZ24], one seems to truly suffer a penalty due to the necessary asymmetry. (For a rough comparison, symmetrizing the best rectangular matrix multiplication algorithms leads to a substantially worse square matrix multiplication algorithm.) However, the gains from the approach above ultimately outweigh the losses from asymmetry.

### 2.4 Our Contributions: More Asymmetry

Following from the sequence of improvements obtained by [DWZ23, VXXZ24], the natural end goal for this line of work is to allow different remaining subtensors to share level- $\ell$ variable blocks in all three dimensions, and only require level- $1$ variable blocks to belong to unique remaining level- $\ell$ subtensors. However, it is unclear how one may achieve this goal since the algorithms of both [DWZ23] and [VXXZ24] crucially use the fact that different remaining level- $\ell$ subtensors use unique level- $\ell$ $X$ - and $Y$ -variable blocks. In this work, we make substantial progress toward this goal by allowing different remaining subtensors to share level- $\ell$ variable blocks in both the $Y$ - and $Z$ -dimensions.

In this work, we give a new approach in which we only require that any two level- $\ell$ subtensors do not share level- $\ell$ $X$ -blocks. In particular, two level- $\ell$ subtensors can share the same level- $\ell$ $Y$ -variable block or $Z$ -variable block, but cannot share the same level- $1$ $Y$ -variable block or $Z$ -variable block, strengthening ideas in [VXXZ24]. In this way, we are able to keep a larger number of level- $\ell$ subtensors and thus zero out the input $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ into more matrix multiplication tensors. This is achieved by introducing more asymmetry into our procedure: we now give a different zeroing-out procedure for each of the $X,Y,Z$ -dimensions. This is perhaps unexpected, because in the end goal all $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -dimensions have the same requirement that every level- $1$ variable block belongs to unique remaining level- $\ell$ subtensors. One might expect that a more symmetric implementation of the ideas of prior work would help towards the goal, but we instead use more asymmetry to get around a major limitation of the prior work.

Compared to the prior works, which use constrained information from both the $X$ - and $Y$ -dimensions to control the $Z$ -dimension, we first use just the $X$ -dimension to partially control the $Y$ -dimension, and then use both the fully-controlled $X$ -dimension and partially-controlled $Y$ -dimension to control the $Z$ -dimension. More specifically, by utilizing more structure specific to the $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ tensor, combined with the requirement that each level- $\ell$ subtensor $T_{IJK}$ uses a unique level- $\ell$ $X$ -block, we find that this already constrains $T_{IJK}$ to use a smaller and more structured subset of level- $1$ $Y$ -blocks, which is sufficient to perform zero-outs over level- $1$ $Y$ -blocks so that each of them is contained in a unique level- $\ell$ subtensor. After obtaining a set of level- $\ell$ subtensors that do not share any level- $\ell$ $X$ -blocks or level- $1$ $Y$ -blocks, we then have enough information to do zero-outs over level- $1$ $Z$ -blocks so that each of them are contained in a unique level- $\ell$ subtensor. See Section 4 for a more detailed overview of our algorithm.

Similar to recent prior matrix multiplication algorithms, we need to solve a large, non-convex optimization problem in order to determine parameters for the laser method to achieve the best exponent. That said, we can already see that our new approach could potentially lead to an improvement without solving the optimization program to get the final bound for $\omega$ . A key parameter that reflects the effectiveness of the laser method is the hash modulus being used in the hashing step standard to all applications of the laser method, which determines the number of remaining level- $\ell$ subtensors we are able to keep in expectation. Minimizing the value of this hash modulus can give an improvement to the bound we are able to obtain for $\omega$ . The new hash modulus we use in this work is taken to be (ignoring low-order terms)

$$ \max\left\{\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BX}}},\frac{N_{\alpha}\cdot p_{\textit{Y},\textup{comp}}}{N_{\textup{BY}}},\frac{N_{\alpha}\cdot p_{\textit{Z},\textup{comp}}}{N_{\textup{BZ}}}\right\}, $$

in comparison with the following value (similarly without low-order terms) used in [VXXZ24]

$$ \max\left\{\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BX}}},\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BY}}},\frac{N_{\alpha}\cdot p_{\textit{Z},\textup{comp}}}{N_{\textup{BZ}}}\right\}. $$

The definitions of all the variables in these expressions are not important for the purpose of this overview, and we focus instead on their structure. Two out of the three terms in the two bounds are the same, but we have improved the middle term from $\frac{N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}}{N_{\textup{BY}}}$ to $\frac{N_{\alpha}\cdot p_{\textit{Y},\textup{comp}}}{N_{\textup{BY}}}$ , where $p_{\textit{Y},\textup{comp}}$ is a variable between $0$ and $1$ which we can pick in our optimization problem. In fact, even in the worst case $p_{\textit{Y},\textup{comp}}=1$ , we improve the second term by a factor of $N_{{\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}}/N_{\alpha}$ , which is guaranteed to be at least $1$ and is exactly the penalty term studied by [AV21]. Thus, even if we pick $p_{\textit{Y},\textup{comp}}=1$ , we would at least recover the modulus of prior work. That said, since the modulus is defined by taking the maximum over the three values, it is not immediately clear that our approach uses a strictly smaller modulus. However, by solving the new constraint program, one can verify that even in $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2}$ , the optimal parameters use a smaller value of $p_{\textit{Y},\textup{comp}}$ , which leads to a better bound on $\omega$ . Indeed, our new approach gives a better analysis of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2}$ than prior work, improving from the bound $\omega<2.374399$ achieved by [DWZ23]55 5 The subsequent work [VXXZ24] improves the analysis of higher powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ but not the square. to $\omega<2.37432$ .

### 2.5 Limitations to Our Techniques

In our approach, we successfully allow all obtained level- $\ell$ subtensors to share level- $k$ variable blocks for any $1<k\leq\ell$ in both the $Y$ - and $Z$ -dimensions, as long as they are independent with respect to the level- $1$ blocks. However, we still require that none of them share level- $\ell$ $X$ -blocks. In an ideal approach, to truly maximize the number of independent tensors, the subtensors should also be allowed to share level- $\ell$ $X$ -blocks as long as they do not share level- $1$ $X$ -blocks. However, there does not seem to be a way to continue our approach to also allow the $X$ blocks to share level- $\ell$ -blocks. Our approach crucially uses the fact that a level- $\ell$ $X$ -block uniquely determines the level- $\ell$ subtensor that it belongs in, to control the structure of level- $1$ blocks in level- $\ell$ subtensors. It seems that a truly new idea is needed to be able to control this structure without making the level- $\ell$ subtensors to have unique level- $\ell$ variable blocks in one of the dimensions. In other words, we believe that we have reached the limit of generalizing the techniques introduced in [DWZ23].

Second, as in all recent improvements, determining the final running time of our matrix multiplication algorithm requires solving a non-convex optimization problem to determine the best choice of the probability distribution $\alpha$ to use in the laser method. Since we can no longer use a symmetry between the $X$ - and $Y$ -dimensions, our new optimization problem has more variables and appears to be considerably harder to solve to high precision than the problems in prior work. It would be particularly exciting to find an approach to improving $\omega$ which does not need powerful optimization software and computing systems.

## 3 Preliminaries

We use by now standard notation as in [AV21, DWZ23, VXXZ24]. The experienced reader may skip this section, as the definitions and notation are the same as in prior work.

### 3.1 Tensors and Tensor Operations

#### Tensors.

We deal with tensors of order $3$ which can be viewed as either $3$ -dimensional arrays or as trilinear polynomials. We consider the latter representation:

A tensor $T$ over variable sets $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{|X|}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{|Y|}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{|Z|}\}$ , and field $\mathbb{F}$ is a trilinear form

$$ T=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k}, $$

where all $a_{i,j,k}$ are from $\mathbb{F}$ .

All tensors in this paper have all their entries $a_{i,j,k}\in\{0,1\}$ . As any field $\mathbb{F}$ has a $0$ and a $1$ , all tensors in the paper can be considered to be over any $\mathbb{F}$ .

In the following, assume $T$ is a tensor over $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{|X|}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{|Y|}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{|Z|}\}$ and $T^{\prime}$ is a tensor over $X^{\prime}=\{x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{|X^{\prime}|}\}$ , $Y^{\prime}=\{y^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,y^{\prime}_{|Y^{\prime}|}\}$ , $Z^{\prime}=\{z^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,z^{\prime}_{|Z^{\prime}|}\}$ , written as

$$ T=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k},\qquad T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X^{\prime}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y^{\prime}|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z^{\prime}|}b_{i,j,k}\cdot x^{\prime}_{i}y^{\prime}_{j}z^{\prime}_{k}, $$

#### Tensor operations.

We define the sum, direct sum, and Kronecker product of two tensors $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ :

- • The sum $T+T^{\prime}$ is only defined when both tensors are over the same variable sets $(X,Y,Z)=(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime})$ . $T+T^{\prime}$ is the tensor defined by the sum of the two polynomials defining $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ :

$$ T+T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}(a_{i,j,k}+b_{i,j,k})\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k}. $$

- • The direct sum $T\oplus T^{\prime}$ is the sum $T+T^{\prime}$ when the variable sets of $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ are disjoint. In this case, $T^{\prime}$ and $T^{\prime}$ are said to be independent. If $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ share variables, we first relabel their variables so that the variable sets are disjoint and then $T\oplus T^{\prime}$ is the sum of the two polynomials over new variables. We write $T^{\oplus n}\coloneqq\underbrace{T\oplus T\oplus\cdots\oplus T}_{n~\textup{copies}}$ to denote the sum of $n$ independent copies66 6 This is often written as $n\odot T$ . of $T$ .

- • The Kronecker product is defined as the tensor

$$ T\otimes T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{|X^{\prime}|}\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{|Y^{\prime}|}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{|Z^{\prime}|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot b_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\cdot(x_{i},x^{\prime}_{i^{\prime}})\cdot(y_{j},y^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}})\cdot(z_{k},z^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}) $$

over variable sets $X\times X^{\prime}$ , $Y\times Y^{\prime}$ , and $Z\times Z^{\prime}$ . We write $T^{\otimes n}\coloneqq\underbrace{T\otimes T\otimes\cdots\otimes T}_{n~\textup{times}}$ to denote the $n$ -th tensor power of $T$ .

- • We say $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ are isomorphic77 7 Note that in the literature, a more general type of isomorphism is considered, where $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ can be transformed into one another under arbitrary linear transformations between $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ , $Y$ and $Y^{\prime}$ , and $Z$ and $Z^{\prime}$ , or even more generally under degenerations., denoted by $T\equiv T^{\prime}$ , if $|X|=|X^{\prime}|$ , $|Y|=|Y^{\prime}|$ , $|Z|=|Z^{\prime}|$ , and there are permutations $\pi_{\textit{X}},\pi_{\textit{Y}},\pi_{\textit{Z}}$ over $[|X|],[|Y|],[|Z|]$ respectively, such that $a_{i,j,k}=b_{\pi_{\textit{X}}(i),\pi_{\textit{Y}}(j),\pi_{\textit{Z}}(k)}$ for all $i,j,k$ . In other words, both tensors are equivalent up to a relabeling of the variables.

### 3.2 Tensor Rank

A tensor $T$ over $X,Y,Z$ has rank $1$ if there are some vectors $a,b,c$ of length $|X|,|Y|,|Z|$ , respectively, so that

$$ T=\Biggl(\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}a_{i}\cdot x_{i}\Biggr)\Biggl(\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}b_{j}\cdot y_{j}\Biggr)\Biggl(\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}c_{k}\cdot z_{k}\Biggr). $$

For a tensor $T$ over $X,Y,Z$ , the tensor rank $R(T)$ is defined to be the minimum integer $r\geq 0$ such that $T$ can be written as the sum of $r$ rank- $1$ tensors. The corresponding sum is called the rank decomposition of $T$ .

Tensor rank satisfies subadditivity and submultiplicativity:

- • $R(T+T^{\prime})\leq R(T)+R(T^{\prime})$ .

- • $R(T\oplus T^{\prime})\leq R(T)+R(T^{\prime})$ .

- • $R(T\otimes T^{\prime})\leq R(T)\cdot R(T^{\prime}).$

The third item above implies that for all $m$ , $R(T^{\otimes m})\leq R(T)^{m}$ , and for many tensors (e.g., $2\times 2$ matrix multiplication) the inequality is strict. Due to Fekete’s lemma, the following asymptotic rank $\tilde{R}(T)$ is well-defined for every tensor $T$ :

$$ \tilde{R}(T)\coloneqq\lim_{m\to\infty}\left(R(T^{\otimes m})\right)^{1/m}. $$

The asymptotic rank is upper bounded by $R(T^{\otimes m})^{1/m}$ for any fixed integer $m>0$ .

### 3.3 Degenerations, Restrictions, Zero-outs

Let $T$ and $T^{\prime}$ be tensors over a field $\mathbb{F}$ , $T$ is over $X,Y,Z$ , and $T^{\prime}$ is over $X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}$ .

#### Degeneration.

Let $\mathbb{F}[\lambda]$ be the ring of polynomials of the formal variable $\lambda$ . We say that $T^{\prime}$ is a degeneration of $T$ , written as $T\unrhd T^{\prime}$ , if there exists $\mathbb{F}[\lambda]$ -linear maps

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{\textit{X}} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(X)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(X^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{\textit{Y}} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Y)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Y^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{\textit{Z}} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Z)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}[\lambda]}(Z^{\prime}), $$

and $d\in\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ T^{\prime}=\lambda^{-d}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot\phi_{\textit{X}}(x_{i})\cdot\phi_{\textit{Y}}(y_{j})\cdot\phi_{\textit{Z}}(z_{k})\right)+O(\lambda). $$

If $T^{\prime}\unrhd T$ , then $\tilde{R}(T^{\prime})\leq\tilde{R}(T)$ .

#### Restriction.

Restriction is a special type of degeneration for the case where the maps $\phi_{\textit{X}},\phi_{\textit{Y}},\phi_{\textit{Z}}$ are $\mathbb{F}$ -linear maps. More specifically, $T^{\prime}$ is a restriction of $T$ if there exist $\mathbb{F}$ -linear maps

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{\textit{X}} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(X)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(X^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{\textit{Y}} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Y)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Y^{\prime}), \displaystyle\phi_{\textit{Z}} \displaystyle:\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Z)\to\textup{span}_{\mathbb{F}}(Z^{\prime}), $$

such that

$$ T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot\phi_{\textit{X}}(x_{i})\cdot\phi_{\textit{Y}}(y_{j})\cdot\phi_{\textit{Z}}(z_{k}). $$

If $T^{\prime}$ is a restriction of $T$ , $R(T^{\prime})\leq R(T)$ , and consequently $\tilde{R}(T^{\prime})\leq\tilde{R}(T)$ .

#### Zero-out.

The laser method utilizes a limited type of restriction called zero-out, namely the maps $\phi_{\textit{X}},\phi_{\textit{Y}},\phi_{\textit{Z}}$ set some variables to zero. More specifically, for subsets $X^{\prime}\subseteq X$ , $Y^{\prime}\subseteq Y$ , $Z^{\prime}\subseteq Z$ we define the maps as

$$ \phi_{\textit{X}}(x_{i})=\begin{cases}x_{i}&\text{If }x_{i}\in X^{\prime},\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

and similarly for $\phi_{\textit{Y}},\phi_{\textit{Z}}$ . The resulting tensor

$$ T^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{i,j,k}\cdot\phi_{\textit{X}}(x_{i})\cdot\phi_{\textit{Y}}(y_{j})\cdot\phi_{\textit{Z}}(z_{k})=\sum_{x_{i}\in X^{\prime}}\sum_{y_{j}\in Y^{\prime}}\sum_{z_{k}\in Z^{\prime}}a_{i,j,k}\cdot x_{i}y_{j}z_{k} $$

is called a zero-out of $T$ . Throughout this paper, we use the notation $T^{\prime}=T|_{X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}}$ to denote the tensor $T^{\prime}$ obtained from $T$ by setting the variables in $X\setminus X^{\prime}$ , $Y\setminus Y^{\prime}$ , $Z\setminus Z^{\prime}$ to zero. In this case, we also call $T^{\prime}$ the subtensor of $T$ over $X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime}$ .

### 3.4 Matrix Multiplication Tensors

For positive integers $a,b,c$ , the $a\times b\times c$ matrix multiplication tensor $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ is a tensor over the variable sets $\{x_{ij}\}_{i\in[a],j\in[b]},\{y_{jk}\}_{j\in[b],k\in[c]},\{z_{ki}\}_{i\in[a],k\in[c]}$ defined as the tensor computing the $a\times c$ (transpose of the) product matrix $\{z_{ki}\}_{i\in[a],k\in[c]}$ of an $a\times b$ matrix $\{x_{ij}\}_{i\in[a],j\in[b]}$ and $b\times c$ matrix $\{y_{jk}\}_{j\in[b],k\in[c]}$ . Specifically,

$$ \langle a,b,c\rangle=\sum_{i\in[a]}\sum_{j\in[b]}\sum_{k\in[c]}x_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ki}. $$

Notice that the coefficient in front of $z_{ki}$ is the $(i,k)$ entry of the product of $x$ with $y$ . It is not hard to check that $\langle a,b,c\rangle\otimes\langle d,e,f\rangle\equiv\langle ad,be,cf\rangle$ .

Following the recursive approach introduced by Strassen in [Str69], for any integer $q\geq 2$ , if $R(\langle q,q,q\rangle)\leq r$ , then one can use the rank decomposition of $\langle q,q,q\rangle$ to design an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\log_{q}(r)})$ to multiply two $n\times n$ matrices. This motivates the definition of the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega$ as follows:

$$ \omega\coloneqq\inf_{q\in\mathbb{N},\,q\geq 2}\log_{q}(R(\langle q,q,q\rangle)). $$

Namely, for every $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\omega+\varepsilon})$ that computes the multiplication of two $n\times n$ matrices. Since $\langle q,q,q\rangle^{\otimes n}\equiv\langle q^{n},q^{n},q^{n}\rangle$ , equivalently $\omega$ can be written in terms of the asymptotic rank of $\langle q,q,q\rangle$ as

$$ \omega=\log_{q}(\tilde{R}(\langle q,q,q\rangle)). $$

We also consider the arithmetic complexity of multiplying rectangular matrices of sizes $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ and $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . We define $\omega(a,b,c)$ as

$$ \omega(a,b,c)=\log_{q}\left(\tilde{R}(\langle q^{a},q^{b},q^{c}\rangle)\right) $$

where $q\geq 2$ is a positive integer. This means that for any $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\omega(a,b,c)+\varepsilon})$ that computes the multiplication of an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ matrix with an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrix.

It is known that $\omega(a,b,c)=\omega(a,c,b)=\omega(c,a,b)$ so that the value remains the same for any permutation of the dimensions $a,b,c$ . In this paper, we focus on bounds for $\omega(1,\kappa,1)$ for $\kappa>0$ .

### 3.5 Schönhage’s Asymptotic Sum Inequality

From a bound $r$ on the rank of any $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ tensor, one can obtain an upper bound $\omega\leq 3\log_{abc}(r)$ . Schönhage [Sch81] extended this fact by showing that one can obtain an upper bound on $\omega$ using any upper bound on the asymptotic rank of a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors:

#### Theorem 3.1 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality [Sch81]).

For positive integers $r>m$ and $a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}$ for $i\in[m]$ , if

$$ \tilde{R}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}\langle a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\rangle\right)\leq r, $$

then $\omega\leq 3\tau$ where $\tau\in[2/3,1]$ is the solution to the equation

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}(a_{i}\cdot b_{i}\cdot c_{i})^{\tau}=r. $$

Analogously, the asymptotic sum inequality can also be used to obtain bounds on the rectangular matrix multiplication as follows.

#### Theorem 3.2 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality for $\omega(a,b,c)$ [Sch81, Blä13]).

Let $t,\,q>0$ be positive integers and $a,b,c\geq 0$ , then

$$ t\cdot q^{\omega(a,b,c)}\leq\tilde{R}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{t}\langle q^{a},q^{b},q^{c}\rangle\right). $$

### 3.6 The Coppersmith-Winograd Tensor

For a nonnegative integer $q\geq 0$ , the Coppersmith-Winograd tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ over the variables $X=\{x_{0},\dots,x_{q+1}\}$ , $Y=\{y_{0},\dots,y_{q+1}\}$ , $Z=\{z_{0},\dots,z_{q+1}\}$ is defined as

$$ \mathrm{CW}_{q}\coloneqq x_{0}y_{0}z_{q+1}+x_{0}y_{q+1}z_{0}+x_{q+1}y_{0}z_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\left(x_{0}y_{i}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{0}z_{i}+x_{i}y_{i}z_{0}\right). $$

Coppersmith and Winograd [CW90] showed that $\tilde{R}(\mathrm{CW}_{q})\leq q+2$ .

Observe that

$$ \mathrm{CW}_{q}\equiv\langle 1,1,q\rangle+\langle q,1,1\rangle+\langle 1,q,1\rangle+\langle 1,1,1\rangle+\langle 1,1,1\rangle+\langle 1,1,1\rangle, $$

where unfortunately “ $+$ ” is a sum and not a direct sum, so that Schönhage’s theorem doesn’t immediately apply. The goal of the laser method is to zero out variables in $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes n}$ so that Schönhage’s theorem can be applied.

### 3.7 Base Leveled Partition of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$

Consider the $2^{\ell-1}$ -th tensor power of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ for $\ell\geq 1$ . For convenience, denote $T^{(\ell)}\coloneqq\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ .

Coppersmith and Winograd [CW90] defined a partitioning of the variables of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ which is used in all following works including [Vas12, AV21, LG14, DWZ23]. We call this the level- $1$ partition. More generally, we describe the leveled partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ which also comes from [CW90] and the subsequent works.

#### Level-1 partition.

For $T^{(1)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , its variable sets $X^{(1)},Y^{(1)},Z^{(1)}$ are partitioned into three parts

$$ \displaystyle X^{(1)} \displaystyle=X^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup X^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup X^{(1)}_{2}=\{x_{0}\}\sqcup\{x_{1},\dots,x_{q}\}\sqcup\{x_{q+1}\}, \displaystyle Y^{(1)} \displaystyle=Y^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup Y^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup Y^{(1)}_{2}=\{y_{0}\}\sqcup\{y_{1},\dots,y_{q}\}\sqcup\{y_{q+1}\}, \displaystyle Z^{(1)} \displaystyle=Z^{(1)}_{0}\sqcup Z^{(1)}_{1}\sqcup Z^{(1)}_{2}=\{z_{0}\}\sqcup\{z_{1},\dots,z_{q}\}\sqcup\{z_{q+1}\}. $$

We denote the subtensor $T^{(1)}\big|_{X^{(1)}_{i},Y^{(1)}_{j},Z^{(1)}_{k}}$ by $T_{i,j,k}^{(1)}$ and we call it a level- $1$ constituent tensor. Note that $T^{(1)}_{i,j,k}$ is nonzero if and only if $i+j+k=2$ . In particular, we can write $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ as a sum of constituent tensors as follows

$$ T^{(1)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k\geq 0\\
i+j+k=2\end{subarray}}T_{i,j,k}^{(1)}. $$

#### Level- $\ell$ partition.

For $T^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}$ with variable sets $X^{(\ell)},Y^{(\ell)},Z^{(\ell)}$ , the above level- $1$ partition on $T^{(1)}$ induces a natural partition on the variable sets $X^{(\ell)},Y^{(\ell)},Z^{(\ell)}$ where parts are indexed by $\{0,1,2\}$ -sequences of length $2^{\ell-1}$ . Specifically, for the $X$ variables we get the partition

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}}X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{1}}\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}}. $$

The partitions for $Y$ - and $Z$ -variables are analogous.

Prior work starting with [CW90] used partitions obtained from the above induced partitions by merging parts whose sequences indices sum to the same number.

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{2^{\ell}}X_{i}^{(\ell)},\qquad\textup{where}\quad X_{i}^{(\ell)}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}\\
\sum_{t}\hat{i}_{t}=i\end{subarray}}X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{1}}\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(1)}_{\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}}. $$

This above partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ is called the level- $\ell$ partition. One can also view this partition as a coarsening of the level-( $\ell-1$ ) partition via merging, i.e.,

$$ X_{i}^{(\ell)}=\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i^{\prime}\leq i\\
0\leq i^{\prime},i-i^{\prime}\leq 2^{\ell-1}\end{subarray}}X^{(\ell-1)}_{i^{\prime}}\otimes X^{(\ell-1)}_{i-i^{\prime}}. $$

The variable sets $Y^{(\ell)}$ and $Z^{(\ell)}$ are partitioned similarly.

Under the level- $\ell$ partition, denote the subtensor $T^{(\ell)}\big|_{X_{i}^{(\ell)},Y_{j}^{(\ell)},Z_{k}^{(\ell)}}$ by $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}$ and call it a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor. Call $X^{(\ell)}_{i},Y^{(\ell)}_{j},Z^{(\ell)}_{k}$ level- $\ell$ variable blocks. We omit the superscript $(\ell)$ when $\ell$ is clear from context.

Note that $T^{(\ell)}_{i,j,k}\neq 0$ if and only if $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ . Thus:

$$ T^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k\geq 0\\
i+j+k=2^{\ell}\end{subarray}}T_{i,j,k}^{(\ell)}. $$

### 3.8 Leveled Partition for Large Tensor Powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$

In the laser method, we focus on a tensor power of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ in the form $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}=(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes n\cdot 2^{\ell-1}}$ . We set $N\coloneqq n\cdot 2^{\ell-1}$ and note that the leveled partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ induces a partition on $(T^{\ell})^{\otimes n}$ . We recall some basic terminology and notation with respect to the leveled partition of $(T^{\ell})^{\otimes n}$ .

#### Level-1 partition of $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ .

In level- $1$ , we view $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ as the tensor $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}$ and consider the partition induced by the level- $1$ partition on $T^{(1)}$ . Each level- $1$ $X$ -variable block $X_{\hat{I}}$ is indexed by a sequence $\hat{I}=(\hat{I}_{1},\dots,\hat{I}_{N})$ of length $N$ in $\{0,1,2\}^{N}$ . The variable block $X_{\hat{I}}$ is defined as

$$ X_{\hat{I}}\coloneqq X_{\hat{I}_{1}}^{(1)}\otimes\dots\otimes X_{\hat{I}_{N}}^{(1)}, $$

where $X_{\hat{I}_{t}}^{(1)}$ for $t\in[N]$ is the level- $1$ partition of $T^{(1)}$ . We call $X_{\hat{I}}$ a level- $1$ variable block and $\hat{I}$ its level- $1$ index sequence. The level- $1$ $Y$ - and $Z$ -variable blocks $Y_{\hat{J}}$ and $Z_{\hat{K}}$ are defined similarly for level- $1$ index sequences $\hat{J},\hat{K}\in\{0,1,2\}^{N}$ . Then notice that $X_{\hat{I}},Y_{\hat{J}},Z_{\hat{K}}$ form a nonzero subtensor of $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}$ if $\hat{I}_{t}+\hat{J}_{t}+\hat{K}_{t}=2$ for all $t\in[N]$ . Thus we write $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}$ as a sum of subtensors

$$ (T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\hat{I},\hat{J},\hat{K}\in\{0,1,2\}^{N}\\
\hat{I}_{t}+\hat{J}_{t}+\hat{K}_{t}=2\,\ \forall t\in[N]\end{subarray}}(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}\big|_{X_{\hat{I}},Y_{\hat{J}},Z_{\hat{K}}}. $$

For convenience, we use $X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}$ to denote the subtensor $(T^{(1)})^{\otimes N}\big|_{X_{\hat{I}},Y_{\hat{J}},Z_{\hat{K}}}$ and we call $X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}$ a level- $1$ triple.

#### Level- $\ell$ partition of $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ .

In level- $\ell$ , we view $(\mathrm{CW}_{q})^{\otimes N}$ as the tensor $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}$ where $n=N/2^{\ell-1}$ and consider the partition induced by the level- $\ell$ partition on $T^{(\ell)}$ . Each level- $1$ $X$ -variable block $X_{I}$ is indexed by a sequence $I\in\{0,1,\dots,2^{\ell}\}^{n}$ of length $n$ . The variable block $X_{I}$ is defined as

$$ X_{I}\coloneqq X_{I_{1}}^{(\ell)}\otimes\dots\otimes X_{I_{n}}^{(\ell)} $$

where $X_{i}^{(\ell)}$ ( $0\leq i\leq 2^{\ell}$ ) is the $i$ -th part in the level- $\ell$ partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ . We call $X_{I}$ a level- $\ell$ variable block and $I$ its level- $\ell$ index sequence. The level- $\ell$ $Y$ - and $Z$ -variable blocks $Y_{J}$ and $Z_{K}$ are defined similarly for level- $\ell$ index sequences $J,K\in\{0,1,\dots,2^{\ell}\}^{n}$ . Similarly, the level- $\ell$ variable blocks $X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}$ form a nonzero subtensor of $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}$ when $I_{t}+J_{t}+K_{t}=2^{\ell}$ for all $t\in[n]$ . So we can write

$$ (T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I,J,K\in\{0,1,2^{\ell}\}^{n}\\
I_{t}+J_{t}+K_{t}=2^{\ell}\,\ \forall t\in[N]\end{subarray}}(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}\big|_{X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}}. $$

As in the level- $1$ partition, for convenience, we use the notation $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ to denote the subtensor $(T^{(\ell)})^{\otimes n}|_{X_{I},Y_{J},Z_{K}}$ and we call such $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ a level- $\ell$ triple.

In addition, note that since the level- $\ell$ partition of $T^{(\ell)}$ is a coarsening of the partition induced by the level- $1$ partition of $T^{(1)}$ , a level- $1$ variable block $X_{\hat{I}}$ is contained in a level- $\ell$ variable block $X_{I}$ if the sequence $I^{\prime}=(I^{\prime}_{1},\dots,I^{\prime}_{n})$ formed by taking $I^{\prime}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+i}$ satisfies $I^{\prime}_{t}=I_{t}$ for all $t\in[n]$ . Namely, if taking the sum of consecutive length- $2^{\ell-1}$ subsequences in $\hat{I}$ yields the sequence $I$ , then $X_{\hat{I}}$ is contained in $X_{I}$ . In this case, we use the notation $\hat{I}\in I$ and $X_{\hat{I}}\in X_{I}$ .

### 3.9 Distributions and Entropy

We only consider distributions with a finite support. Let $\alpha$ be a distribution supported on a set $S$ , i.e., we have $\alpha(s)\geq 0$ for all $s\in S$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\alpha(s)=1$ . The entropy of $\alpha$ , denoted as $H(\alpha)$ , is defined as

$$ H(\alpha)\coloneqq-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in S\\
\alpha(s)>0\end{subarray}}\alpha(s)\log\alpha(s), $$

where the $\log$ has base $2$ . We use the following well-known combinatorial fact.

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $\alpha$ be a distribution over the set $[s]=\{1,\dots,s\}$ . Let $N>0$ be a positive integer, then we have

$$ \binom{N}{\alpha(1)N,\dots,\alpha(s)N}=2^{N(H(\alpha)\pm o(1))}. $$

For two distributions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ over the sets $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ respectively, we define the joint distribution $\alpha\times\beta$ as the distribution over $S\times S^{\prime}=\{(s,s^{\prime})\mid s\in S,\,s^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}\}$ such that

$$ (\alpha\times\beta)(s,s^{\prime})=\alpha(s)\cdot\beta(s^{\prime}). $$

When $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ are sets of integer sequences, we will instead define $\alpha\times\beta$ as a distribution over all integer sequences that can be obtained by concatenating one sequence in $S$ and one sequence in $S^{\prime}$ , such that

$$ (\alpha\times\beta)(s\circ s^{\prime})=\alpha(s)\cdot\beta(s^{\prime}), $$

where $s\circ s^{\prime}$ denotes the concatenation of $s$ and $s^{\prime}$ .

### 3.10 Complete Split Distributions

Motivated by the leveled partition of tensor powers of $\mathrm{CW}_{q}$ , the complete split distribution is defined to characterize the level- $1$ variable blocks contained in level- $\ell$ variable blocks. (Complete split distributions were first defined and used by [VXXZ24].)

#### Definition 3.4 (Complete Split Distribution).

A complete split distribution for a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}$ with $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ is a distribution on all length $2^{\ell-1}$ sequences $(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ .

For a level- $1$ index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ , we say that it is consistent with a complete split distribution $\beta$ if the proportion of any index sequence $(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ in

$$ \left\{\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}\;\middle|\;t\in[n]\right\} $$

equals $\beta(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})$ . Namely, for every $(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ , we have

$$ \left\lvert\left\{t\in[n]\;\middle|\;\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}=(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\right\}\right\rvert=\beta(\hat{i}_{1},\hat{i}_{2},\ldots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\cdot n. $$

Notice that any level-1 index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ defines a complete split distribution by computing the proportion of each type of length- $2^{\ell-1}$ consecutive chunks present in $\hat{I}$ . More specifically, we have the following definition.

#### Definition 3.5.

Given a level-1 index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ , its complete split distribution over $(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ is defined as

$$ \textsf{{split}}\bigl(\hat{I}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\left\lvert\left\{t\in[n]\;\middle|\;\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}=\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)\right\}\right\rvert. $$

Given a subset $S\subseteq[n]$ , we can define the complete split distribution over $(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}})\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ given by $\hat{I}$ restricted to the subset $S$ as

$$ \textsf{{split}}\bigl(\hat{I},S\bigr)\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)=\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot\left\lvert\left\{t\in S\;\middle|\;\bigl(\hat{I}_{(t-1)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}+p}\bigr)_{p=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}=\bigl(\hat{i}_{1},\dots,\hat{i}_{2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)\right\}\right\rvert. $$

Given two complete split distributions $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ over the length- $2^{\ell-1}$ index sequences $\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ , the $L_{\infty}$ distance between $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ is defined to be

$$ \left\lVert\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\max_{\sigma\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}}|\beta_{1}(\sigma)-\beta_{2}(\sigma)|. $$

For any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a fixed complete split distribution $\beta$ , we say that a level-1 index sequence $\hat{I}\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}\cdot n}$ is consistent with $\beta$ up to $\varepsilon$ error if $\lVert\textsf{{split}}(\hat{I})-\beta\rVert_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon$ . When the $\varepsilon$ is clear from context, we say that $\hat{I}$ is approximately consistent with $\beta$ if it is consistent with $\beta$ up to $\varepsilon$ error.

#### Definition 3.6.

For a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor $T_{i,j,k}$ , an integer exponent $N$ , a constant $\varepsilon\geq 0$ , and three complete split distributions $\beta_{\textit{X}},\beta_{\textit{Y}},\beta_{\textit{Z}}$ for the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables respectively, we define

$$ T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}[\beta_{\textit{X}},\beta_{\textit{Y}},\beta_{\textit{Z}},\varepsilon]\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{level-}1\text{ triple }X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}\textup{ in }T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}\\
\hat{I}\text{ approximately consistent with }\beta_{\textit{X}}\\
\hat{J}\text{ approximately consistent with }\beta_{\textit{Y}}\\
\hat{K}\text{ approximately consistent with }\beta_{\textit{Z}}\end{subarray}}X_{\hat{I}}Y_{\hat{J}}Z_{\hat{K}}. $$

It is a subtensor of $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}$ over all level-1 $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variable blocks that are approximately consistent with $\beta_{\textit{X}}$ , $\beta_{\textit{Y}}$ , $\beta_{\textit{Z}}$ , respectively. When $\varepsilon=0$ , we will simplify the notation to $T_{i,j,k}^{\otimes N}[\beta_{\textit{X}},\beta_{\textit{Y}},\beta_{\textit{Z}}]$ .

### 3.11 Salem-Spencer Sets

In the hashing step of the laser method, we make use of the existence of a large subset of $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ that avoids $3$ -term arithmetic progressions, as given by Salem and Spencer [SS42] and improved by Behrend [Beh46].

#### Theorem 3.7 ([Beh46, EHPS24]).

For every positive integer $M>0$ , there exists a subset $B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ of size

$$ |B|\geq M\cdot e^{-O(\sqrt{\log M})}=M^{1-o(1)} $$

that contains no nontrivial $3$ -term arithmetic progressions. Specifically, any $a,b,c\in B$ satisfy $a+b\equiv 2c\pmod{M}$ if and only if $a=b=c$ .

## 4 Algorithm Outline

Our high-level framework is similar to previous works [DWZ23, VXXZ24], and we borrow definitions such as interface tensors, compatibility, and usefulness. We begin by defining the notion of interface tensors, which captures the structure of the intermediate tensors we obtain from different stages of our algorithm and pass to the next stages.

#### Definition 4.1 (Interface Tensor).

For a positive integer $\ell\geq 1$ and any constant $0\leq\varepsilon\leq 1$ , a level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon$ -interface tensor $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ with parameter list

$$ \{(n_{t},i_{t},j_{t},k_{t},\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t})\}_{t\in[s]} $$

is defined as

$$ \mathcal{T}^{*}\coloneqq\bigotimes_{t=1}^{s}T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t},\varepsilon], $$

where $i_{t}+j_{t}+k_{t}=2^{\ell}$ for every $t\in[s]$ (i.e., $T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}$ is a level- $\ell$ constituent tensor) and $\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t}$ are level- $\ell$ complete split distributions for $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variables respectively. We call each $T_{i_{t},j_{t},k_{t}}^{\otimes n_{t}}[\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t},\varepsilon]$ a term of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ . When $\varepsilon=0$ , we will simply call $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ a level- $\ell$ interface tensor.

Our algorithm takes $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell^{*}-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ as input, and applies the global stage of the algorithm described in Section 5 to degenerate it into independent copies of a level- $\ell^{*}$ $\varepsilon_{\ell^{*}}$ -interface tensor. For every $\ell\in[\ell^{*}]$ , we will have a parameter $\varepsilon_{\ell}$ controlling the error margin of level- $\ell$ interface tensors. Then for $\ell=\ell^{*},\ell^{*}\!-\!1,\ldots,2$ , we apply the constituent stage of the algorithm described in Section 6 to degenerate a level- $\ell$ $\varepsilon_{\ell}$ -interface tensor into a tensor product between independent copies of level- $(\ell-1)$ $\varepsilon_{\ell-1}$ -interface tensors and a matrix multiplication tensor. Eventually, we obtain a tensor product between independent copies of level- $1$ $\varepsilon_{1}$ -interface tensors and a matrix multiplication tensor, which can then be degenerated into independent copies of matrix multiplication tensors. Thus, the overall algorithm degenerates $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell^{*}-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ into independent copies of matrix multiplication tensors as desired.

### 4.1 Algorithm Outline

The framework for the constituent stage is similar to the framework for the global stage. For simplicity, we only present the outline of our global stage algorithm for $\varepsilon=0$ as it captures the main ideas of our algorithm and illustrates the main differences between our algorithm and [VXXZ24]’s. A high-level comparison between our algorithm and [VXXZ24]’s is provided in Fig. 1.

*Figure 1: Main differences between the global stage algorithm in [VXXZ24] and this work as outlined in Section 4.1. Other technical differences are omitted.*

As mentioned earlier, the goal of the global stage is to take $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ as input (for convenience, we will use $\ell$ to denote $\ell^{*}$ ), and output a set of level- $1$ -independent level- $\ell$ interface tensors. Since our algorithm treats the $X,Y,Z$ dimensions asymmetrically and there are six permutations of the $X,Y,Z$ dimensions, we can essentially apply our algorithm in six different ways. As a result, we will split $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ into $\bigotimes_{r\in[6]}\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{r}\cdot n}$ for some $A_{1},\ldots,A_{6}\geq 0$ and $\sum_{r=1}^{6}A_{r}=1$ , where we call each $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes A_{r}\cdot n}$ a region. We apply our algorithm for each permutation of the $X,Y,Z$ dimensions on one of the regions. We note that in [VXXZ24], two of the three dimensions are treated symmetrically, so they only need to split the input tensor into $3$ regions instead of $6$ . For simplicity, we outline each step of our algorithm on a fixed permutation without splitting $\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ into regions in the following.

- 1. Zero-out according to $\alpha$ . This is a standard first step present in all previous applications of the laser method. For some distribution $\alpha$ over level- $\ell$ constituent tensors, let ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ be the marginal distributions of $\alpha$ on the $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -dimensions respectively. We zero out $X$ -, $Y$ -, $Z$ -variable blocks that are not consistent with ${\alpha}_{\textit{X}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Y}},{\alpha}_{\textit{Z}}$ respectively.

- 2. Asymmetric hashing. Similar to [DWZ23, VXXZ24], we then apply asymmetric hashing. Unlike previous works, where after the asymmetric hashing each level- $\ell$ $X$ -variable block $X_{I}$ or $Y$ -variable block $Y_{J}$ is contained in a unique level- $\ell$ triple $X_{I}Y_{J}Z_{K}$ , we only require each level- $\ell$ $X$ -block to be contained in a unique triple. Moreover, the number of triples containing each level- $\ell$ $Y$ -block is at most the number of triples containing each level- $\ell$ $Z$ -block.

- 3. $Y$ -compatibility zero-outs. In [DWZ23, VXXZ24], the next step is to do some zeroing outs based on a notion of compatibility defined for level- $1$ $Z$ -blocks, provided that every level- $1$ $X$ - and $Y$ -block is contained in a unique block triple. So in our algorithm, we first need to ensure that each level- $1$ $Y$ -block is contained in a unique block triple by performing the following sub-steps. Note that our goal is to obtain an interface tensor with $\left\{\beta_{\textit{X},i,j,k},\beta_{\textit{Y},i,j,k},\beta_{\textit{Z},i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ as its complete split distributions. Since each level- $\ell$ $X$ -block is contained in a unique block triple, we are already able to identify the subset of indices $t$ with $X_{t}=i$ , $Y_{t}=j$ , $Z_{t}=k$ for every $i,j,k$ . This means that we can compute the complete split distributions for each level- $1$ $X$ -block with respect to these indices, and zero out any level- $1$ $X$ -block that is not consistent with $\left\{\beta_{\textit{X},i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ . (a) $Y$ -compatibility zero-out I. Then we define a notion of compatibility for a level- $1$ $Y$ -block with respect to a level- $\ell$ block triple containing it. We say a level- $1$ $Y$ -block is compatible with a level- $\ell$ block triple if they satisfy the compatibility conditions. We zero out all level- $1$ $Y$ -blocks that are not compatible with any triple. (b) $Y$ -compatibility zero-out II. In this step, we zero out the level- $1$ $Y$ -blocks that are compatible with more than one triple. After this step, we can ensure that each level- $1$ $Y$ -block is contained in a unique level- $\ell$ block triple and it is compatible with that triple. (c) $Y$ -usefulness zero-out. At this point, each level- $1$ $Y$ -block is contained in a unique triple, so we can zero out a level- $1$ $Y$ -block if it is not consistent with $\left\{\beta_{\textit{Y},i,j,k}\right\}_{i+j+k=2^{\ell}}$ , similar to what we did to the level- $1$ $X$ -blocks.

- 4. $Z$ -compatibility zero-outs. Although after the more asymmetric hashing step, we only have $X$ -blocks in a unique triple, notice that after $Y$ -compatibility zero-outs, we achieve the property that now every level- $1$ $X$ - and $Y$ -block is compatible with a unique level- $\ell$ triple. This property is weaker than the property achieved in [DWZ23, VXXZ24] after their original asymmetric hashing steps, but this is sufficient for later steps. In particular, in our $Z$ -compatibility zero-out, we can perform essentially the same procedure as in [VXXZ24] to achieve the property that every level- $1$ $Z$ -block is compatible with a unique level- $\ell$ triple.

- 5. Fixing holes. Now every level- $1$ block is contained in a unique level- $\ell$ triple, but some of the level- $1$ blocks we zeroed out in $Y$ -compatibility zero-outs and $Z$ -compatibility zero-outs become holes, i.e., the copies of the interface tensors we obtain miss some variables due to the compatibility zero-outs. We use the following result to fix these holes. Theorem 4.2 ([VXXZ24, Corollary 3.2]). Let $T$ be a level- $\ell$ interface tensor with parameter list

$$ \{(n_{t},i_{t},j_{t},k_{t},\beta_{\textit{X},t},\beta_{\textit{Y},t},\beta_{\textit{Z},t})\}_{t\in[s]}. $$

Let $N=2^{\ell-1}\cdot\sum_{t\in[s]}n_{t}$ . Suppose $T_{1},\dots,T_{r}$ are broken copies of $T$ where $\leq\frac{1}{8N}$ fraction of level-1 $X$ , $Y$ , and $Z$ -blocks are holes. If $r\geq 2^{C_{1}N/\log N}$ for some large enough constant $C_{1}>0$ , the direct sum $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}T_{i}$ can degenerate into an unbroken copy of $T$ .

## 5 Global Stage

For our global stage algorithm, the input is the tensor $\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes N}$ where $N=n\cdot 2^{\ell^{*}-1}$ . The algorithm will output a set of independent copies of level- $\ell^{*}$ interface tensors that are degenerated from the input tensor. For convenience, we use $\ell$ to denote $\ell^{*}$ in the rest of this section.

Given a distribution $\alpha$ over the set $\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3}\mid i+j+k=2^{\ell}\}$ and level- $\ell$ complete split distributions $\beta_{\textit{X},i,j,k}$ , $\beta_{\textit{Y},i,j,k}$ , $\beta_{\textit{Z},i,j,k}$ we define the quantities listed in Table 2.

#### Proposition 5.1.

$\bigl(\mathrm{CW}_{q}^{\otimes 2^{\ell-1}}\bigr)^{\otimes n}$ can be degenerated into a direct sum of $2^{(\sum_{r=1}^{6}A_{r}E_{r})n-o(n)}$ copies of a level- $\ell$ interface tensor with parameter list

$$ \left\{\left(n\cdot A_{r}\cdot\alpha^{(r)}(i,j,k),i,j,k,\beta_{\textit{X},i,j,k}^{(r)},\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Y},i,j,k},\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Z},i,j,k}\right)\right\}_{r\in[6],\,i+j+k=2^{\ell}} $$

where

- • $0\leq A_{r}\leq 1$ , $\sum_{r=1}^{6}A_{r}=1$ ;

- • $\alpha^{(r)}$ for every $r\in[6]$ is a distribution over $\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3}\mid i+j+k=2^{\ell}\}$ ;

- • For every $W\in\{X,Y,Z\}$ , $\beta_{\textit{W},i,j,k}^{(r)}$ for $r\in[6]$ , $i+j+k=2^{\ell}$ is a level- $\ell$ complete split distribution;

- • For each $r\in[6]$ , define $\pi_{r}:\{X,Y,Z\}\to\{X,Y,Z\}$ as the $r$ -th permutation in the lexicographic order. Then

$$ E_{r}\coloneqq\min\left\{H\Bigl(\alpha_{\pi_{r}(X)}^{(r)}\Bigr)-P_{\alpha}^{(r)},H\Bigl(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{\pi_{r}(Y),*,*,*}^{(r)}\Bigr)-\eta_{\pi_{r}(Y)}^{(r)},H\Bigl(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{\pi_{r}(Z),*,*,*}^{(r)}\Bigr)-\lambda_{\pi_{r}(Z)}^{(r)}\right\}. $$

The following remark illustrates some simple relationships between the complete split distributions for the $X$ , $Y$ , $Z$ -dimensions that we can assume without loss of generality, which will be useful in our algorithms.

#### Remark 5.2 ([VXXZ24]).

Without loss of generality, we can assume that, for every $r,i,j,k$ , and every $L\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}$ ,

$$ \beta^{(r)}_{\textit{X},i,0,k}(L)=\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Z},i,0,k}(\vec{2}-L),\quad\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Z},0,j,k}(L)=\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Y},0,j,k}(\vec{2}-L),\quad\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Y},i,j,0}(L)=\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{X},i,j,0}(\vec{2}-L), $$

where $\vec{2}$ denotes the length- $(2^{\ell-1})$ vector whose coordinates are all $2$ , and

$$ \beta^{(r)}_{\textit{X},i,j,k}(L)=0\text{ if }\sum_{t}L_{t}\neq i,\quad\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Y},i,j,k}(L)=0\text{ if }\sum_{t}L_{t}\neq j,\quad\beta^{(r)}_{\textit{Z},i,j,k}(L)=0\text{ if }\sum_{t}L_{t}\neq k, $$

because otherwise, the level- $\ell$ interface tensor will be the zero tensor and the lemma will follow trivially.
